en: *The Collection of Causes and Conditions for Virtue and Transgression in the Nature of Mind*,
Volume One (Upper) Annotated by Chan Master Zhijue of the Great Song Dynasty I prostrate my head before the Buddha of the Three Bodies,
The teachings of Exoteric and Esoteric, Half and Full, And the noble Sangha of the Three Vehicles.
And those who protect the True Dharma—I shall now briefly record and preserve for them. As for the causes and conditions of the mind’s nature regarding sin and merit, I have not recorded them here;
for the scriptural texts are already explicit, and the words of the Sages are clearly set forth within their treatises.
After the Muni has entered Nirvāṇa and the True Dharma has come to an end...
The people of the Five Indies and the borderlands, the fourfold assembly of recent times—whether they be heterodox or orthodox, faithful or faithless—the wise should all examine them.

Therefore, whether from what I have personally seen or heard from others, I have recorded but a small portion for the sake of admonishing and encouraging future generations; may those who see or hear this refrain from praise or slander.

If there are disciples of the fourfold assembly who enter together into the ocean of the Dharma-nature, desiring to leave birth and death behind and realize great *nirvāṇa*, then even if they lack dignified deportment and have violated the precepts,
they must certainly contemplate the inconceivable merits, marks, signs, supernormal powers, wisdom, and compassion of the three bodies (*trikāya*).
Deliberating on the principle, one cites scriptural evidence to make known the merits and benefits.
Regarding the contemplation of the merits of the three bodies: in the country of Central India, there was a śramaṇa named Saṃghadatta.
By his natural disposition, he was indolent and lazy; although he had received full ordination, he either did not know the rules of what to observe and what to avoid, nor did he engage in recitation.

Though they recite the sūtras and teach the mantras, they accept offerings from the faithful while spending their days and nights in vain. Their three karmas frequently transgress the precepts, and they commit offenses throughout the six periods of the day.

Lacking shame and remorse, they feel no dread for the future life. When the resident monks of the monastery—both elders and juniors—see that such a person has broken the precepts, they will not allow them to share a seat with them;
they may even drive them away and expel them from within the temple. Yet, this bhikṣu possesses a small portion [of merit].
Wisdom: It discerns the characteristics of the merits of the three bodies (*trikāya*). Day and night, one constantly contemplates the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

Within a single thought-moment, the wisdom of the suchness of phenomena (*dharmatathatājñāna*) and the objective realm of the suchness of phenomena are spontaneously and fully present, adorned with myriad virtues.

Due to false clinging, one sinks into the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*); yet in every thought-moment—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—all are the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). One should constantly contemplate the Dharma.
In its nature, it requires no other dharmas. Thereupon, as the bhikṣu gradually grew old and infirm, he suffered from illness for months. Those who saw him in the saṃgha did not fail to revile him.
At the time of his death, transformation Buddhas and Bodhisattvas came to his side and preached the Dharma of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
The bhikṣu rejoiced, his countenance became bright and pure, and with right mindfulness and composure, he was reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven, where his radiance was extraordinary.
The fragrance pervaded the entire kingdom. When the assembly of bhikṣus, as well as men and women, beheld such meritorious qualities of this bhikṣu, they shed tears of sympathetic joy.
They apologized for their previous slanders, repented their transgressions with shame, and resolved to practice contemplation on the merits of the three bodies (trikāya).
Those who engaged in such cultivation were exceedingly numerous. Therefore, one should know that the Buddha, the sentient beings, and the mind are non-dual.
"Separate. You should contemplate the quiescent true suchness (tathatā) of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), for all dharmas are inconceivable.
"Listen also, you two elderly monks who play go: formerly, in our search for the Way, we traveled through various lands."
In the kingdom of Jiu-liu, there was a great monastery with seven hundred monks who studied both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings and all propagated the Buddha-dharma.
In one of the monastic cells lived two elderly monks whose sole delight was the game of *weiqi*.

With one mind, the two monks spent their days and nights engaged in the pastime of *weiqi*, harboring no other thoughts; they did not seek out the scriptures or teachings, nor did they cultivate the Path.
Among the monastics and laypeople who observed this, there was none who did not voice their censure. I heard that this was done to test his mind. I went to where the two elder monks were;
however, the two elders did not greet me, as they were deeply absorbed in a game of *weiqi* (go) and had not turned their attention to external objects.

Seeking an opportunity for conversation, I said to the elder monks, "I have come seeking the Dharma, traveling from the eastern desert sands to the Five Indias, yet I have not yet entered the stream of the Dharma. My heart—
My nature was parched, like a thirsty deer rushing about in search of water. "I pray that you two Great Beings will bestow the great water of the Dharma upon my thirsting heart.
Weeping and lamenting with grief, the two elder śramaṇas perceived my profound resolve; they spread out seats for us and bade us sit. They then spoke to me, saying:
"The two of us are already advanced in years. Our occupation has been playing go (chess) throughout our lives until old age."
The Dharma Master was traveling. The multitude rebuked him, saying: "The resolve of the Sage is firm as he seeks Great Bodhi; yet we still sigh that he has not yet transcended birth and death.
Why do you instruct this śramaṇa to seek the fruit of Buddhahood? He has come from afar only to forcefully demand the Buddha-dharma;

seeing that his faith is not granted, he will surely act contrary to the Buddha’s intent. If this śramaṇa truly desires to weary of birth and death, he should contemplate the true mark (dharmatā). He may...
Contemplating the nature of the mind: we two have taken the game of Go as our object of focus to seek the Buddha-dharma and observe the nature of the mind.
As the years have passed and the days have deepened, we still do not know the proper method. How much more so if one abandons the contemplation of the mind—how could one seek the path of the Buddha?

To reveal its characteristics so that you may enter the waters of the Dharma: the True Suchness of the Buddha-realm is like a Go board; the distinctions of the nine realms are like the nine black dots. The multitude...

The world of sentient beings, the world of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), and the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*) are distinguished by manifold layers of differentiation, like the three hundred and sixty channels of the eyes.

Impurity, counting the breath, the five faculties (*pañcendriya*), the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*), the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*), the four means of attraction (*catuḥsaṃgrahavastu*), the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), and the three mindfulnesses (*tri-smṛti*):

such dharma-gates are like a small amount of white stone. The three poisons, the seven types of pride (*saptamāna*), the five hindrances (*pañcanīvaraṇa*), the ten envelopments (*daśasaṃyojana*), the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅgapratītyasamutpāda*), and the eight [wrong paths]...
The eight wrong paths and the eight difficulties are thus formed by evil dharmas and black karma, like black pebbles.

When the clarity of the wisdom-mind subdues the delusions of ignorance, it is like striking and destroying the black pebble with a white stone. When the mind of ignorance loses its way and destroys the seeds of bodhi, it is like the black pebble striking and destroying the white stone.
When the resolve for the Way is firm and wisdom is clear, one shatters the enemy of afflictions until they are exhausted.
It is known that the dharma-realm is like a black stone: all are struck and destroyed, leaving only white stones filling the platter.

When afflictions erupt violently, with false views and unwholesomeness such that not a single fraction of goodness remains—such as the person of icchantika who goes from darkness into darkness with no prospect of escape—it is just as when all the white stones are struck and destroyed, leaving only black stones filling the platter. Thus it is.
Delusion, affliction, and birth-and-death—thus one cultivates bodhi and nirvāṇa.
These are never separate from the *tathatā* dharma-dhātu, just as white and black stones on a board have their respective victories and defeats yet remain inseparable.
Just so, observe delusion and awakening moment by moment; seek the principle of suchness (*tathatā*), and the three bodies (*trikāya*) will reside within the mind. It cannot be... [omitted].
Seek it externally; True Suchness (Tathatā) possesses the body. Why seek it elsewhere? Take this single Dharma alone as the object of contemplation.

Remotely take the Dharma-realm as your object, pervading the ten directions. The multitudes do not know this and deeply reproach us; yet by taking these contrary conditions as seeds, we cause the sprout of Buddhahood to germinate.
You, Great Śramaṇa, be careful in practicing this teaching; do not let others know of it. The foolish are deluded by its profundity, which increases their cycle of rebirth.
"Turning away from suffering. The wise understand deeply and penetrate both sin and merit. Strive! Strive! This must be firmly believed and accepted; it must not be disclosed.
We shall cause you to gain even greater conviction for your sake, because the power of contemplating the mind is inconceivable.
Having finished speaking these words, he sat in silence. Suddenly, the two monks vanished, and no one knew where they had gone. The chess pieces were likewise lost.
They departed. Five-colored light filled the chamber. Witnessing such a rare occurrence, I rejoiced with palms joined, weeping as I prostrated myself in homage.
With longing and devotion, I followed and praised the two monks. Before even a single hour had passed, they suddenly appeared before me.
Seated upon their thrones, the two monks further admonished me: "Contemplate the nature of the Tathāgata; it is not separate from your own mind. Its merit and majesty—"
"The deity still remains thus. Return to your native land and cultivate meditative practice deeply; you must come to loathe birth and death. Thus did he exhort me.
Having received these instructions, although I conceived deep faith, I did not yet know the nature of the mind. "This is a secret matter; do not speak of it to the foolish.

Therefore, one should know that there is no difference between the three—mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—and that one should contemplate the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the dharma-nature as quiescent.
Quiescence. Because the arising of the mind regarding all phenomena is inconceivable.
The Chan Master Daojue rebuked a lazy bhikṣu, saying: "You possess past affinities that have led you to be born in this life;
fortunately, you have encountered the Buddha-dharma, yet you have not tasted its nectar. In this single lifetime, you have fled as swiftly as thunder."
A flash of lightning! A venomous snake coiled around your body—why do you not feel fear? To sleep in the same bed as a murderous enemy and yet live in peace?

How much more so when the messengers of Yama press upon you from the dark path, and the King of Impermanence acts as your guide through birth and death? Like a shadow following its form, he hastens your end; you do not realize it.
Why are you attached to pleasure and fail to perceive impermanence? You remain steeped in sleep throughout the night, failing to cultivate the Dharma. Sleep!
Sleep is to be loathed as the root of indolence; breaking the precepts is to be ashamed of as the very source of birth and death.
I recall that in the past, when I was seeking the Buddha-dharma, I traveled to and stayed in the kingdom of Kucha. At one time, I spent a night lodging in the mountains.
When midnight arrived, there suddenly arose the sound of weeping and crying out. The voice proclaimed: "Many thieves are seizing me!"
Wealth, yet I do not know the way to depart. Alas, alas! My strength is now exhausted. Neighboring men and women of compassionate nature, please assist my body and save my life!
At that time, hearing this sound of lamentation and weeping, I started up in alarm and rushed out to see and hear what was happening.
The men and women, monks and nuns, noble and humble alike within the village, all awakened from their dreams and gathered for a council.
He said, "I have seen this holy man for over forty years dwelling in huts made of woven grass, possessing only the three robes and a single alms bowl—just enough to sustain his life.
He relies solely on alms-gathering; he wears discarded rags and never fine garments.
What wealth or treasure could a robber steal from him? This is truly extraordinary. We should go visit him. That night, the people gathered before the bhikṣu.
The bhikṣu shed tears and said to the people: "For many years past, I have sought Bodhi; I have exhaustively searched the scriptures and teachings, constantly brushing away the dust of doubt.
At night, I have ceased sleep and deeply clarified my contemplation of the mind. Thus, for more than forty years, I have not retreated.
Yet tonight, the various enemies that are the afflictions have entered. During the first watch of the night, I sat upright and contemplated the Three Truths."

Principle: Distraction and craving arise in competition, not as exceptions, as they forcibly seize the wealth of the Dharma. Hardly have I turned back through skillful means when the practice of contemplation begins again.
The powerful thief of sleep oppresses my mind, stealing at will the various treasures of the Dharma—faith, power, diligence, the factors of awakening, compassion, samādhi, and liberation.
Now that dawn has broken, I awaken to this and weep bitterly, sighing with deep lamentation. I reflect...
There is not even a fraction of benefit [to be gained]. You, the great assembly, should save my body! I have no one to rely upon, for my dharma-treasures are exhausted;
I am filled with dread, for I am beset by enemies and bandits. Shedding tears and prostrating myself, I look up to heaven and bow down to the earth, sighing in boundless sorrow.
Everyone who saw or heard of this, whether they were great or small, was moved by grief. I have received the instructions of that Sage through his compassionate mindfulness;
thus, I see you now after more than forty years of slumber. The wise sigh deeply in lamentation: why do you not give rise to a heart of shame and remorse?
Quickly take up faith and do not give rise to indolence. When a bhikṣu suddenly hears the Great Master’s reproach, he feels deep shame and fear regarding his transgressions;

by contemplating the principle of the nature of the mind, he perceives the Buddha in his own person. Therefore, one should know that the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings are three things without distinction.
One should contemplate that the *dharmatā* and *tathatā* are quiescent, for the arising of all phenomena from the mind is inconceivable.

○ Regarding conduct according to the mind, you should also hear this: In the past, when I traveled to the land of Hu to pay homage to various monasteries, I stayed in one monastery and heard of the karma performed by a certain monk.
He did not remain in a single place for even a moment, much less for a long duration.
[He may see them] for a single day or even for a year. He sees those facing east turning toward the south; he sees those facing south turning again toward the north.
He sees those standing while gazing up at the sky suddenly prostrate themselves, looking at the ground. He sees those who were walking suddenly sitting peacefully;
he sees those who were sitting upright suddenly lying down with their pillows high. Some are putting on clothes, some are taking off their clothes; some are assuming dignified deportment, or...
Incomplete; or again, they may dance and sing and yet weep with sorrow; or they may eat much, or else abstain from food; or they may carry bows and arrows, or carry a mendicant’s staff;
or they may wear fine garments, or wear robes of rags from the dustheap; suddenly they praise others, and suddenly they revile them;
for a moment their voices are loud, and for a moment they are silent; or again, they may recite scriptures, or perform prostrations—moment by moment.
Even after a single period of time, his coarse and unruly behavior remained just as it was; how much more so day after day, even year after year?

His conduct was so unstable that it cannot be described. When the monks within the monastery saw or heard of him interacting with men and women, they did not consider him an ordinary person, but rather called him a deluded and utterly mad man. When I went to see him, I felt deep astonishment.
For three or four days, I followed this man, yet I could not understand his intent. With a sincere heart, I paid homage to the mad bhikṣu.
Moved by great compassion, the Great Master drew me toward him. Suddenly, upon hearing my words finished, the bhikṣu left the monastery and went into a secluded forest.
I observed his movements and followed the mad monk’s path; when the mad monk reached the edge of the forest, he sat down.
Beneath a tree, he spoke to me, saying: "O Śramaṇa, son of the Dharma, great spiritual friend, you have come with a sincere heart to seek the path to Bodhi.
Listen with a devoted mind, receive it with faith, and do not oppose it. If you wish to seek Buddhahood, you must minutely examine the mind.
Deep in the sleep of ignorance, delusive thoughts arise like dreams; the nature of the mind is frantic and deluded, not abiding for even a single kṣaṇa, just like a restless monkey."
A single tree, like flowing water, does not remain for even a moment. Because of this, various realms of existence arise falsely and differently.

Through the karma of good and evil, one may experience happiness after being born in heaven, yet return to be born in hell; one may occupy the throne of a Wheel-Turning King with the seven treasures complete, yet return to be born into a poor household;
one may be solitary and filled with distress; or having been born as a lion, though it subdues all other beasts, it may still be born as an ant, timid and weak.

It is powerless. Thus, these differences arise from the deluded mind. If one seeks its original nature, it is immovable and tranquil, beyond the realm of words and free from the characteristics of thought.
To observe in this way is to be a true child of the Buddha. My own fundamental mind-nature suffers from a heavy illness of distraction;
because the practice of counting the breath is difficult to apply as an antidote, for this reason I follow my original inclination and observe the mind.
Through subtle contemplation of deluded thoughts, I observe that the nature of the mind does not abide for even a single moment, but transforms with every instant according to its objects.
Following whatever the mind conceives, it manifests my own deportment. Although it thus revolves, its essence remains unseen; this is inconceivable, yet it is not that there is nothing known.
Only a Buddha exhaustively realizes the fundamental source of the nature of the mind. It has been more than twenty years since I first resolved upon the Bodhi-mind. From the beginning...

From the time I first resolved my mind [for enlightenment] until this day, my delusive thoughts have followed their course without concealing my faults; yet, when I search for them minutely and investigate them, they can no longer be found.
Nevertheless, I practice according to what the Tathāgata has taught. Although the illness of my afflictions is grave, I simply follow the nature of that fundamental illness;

thus, by following the mind with mastery, it naturally becomes subdued. It is like catching a turtle or a fish: once it is on the hook, it is cast aside; whether it floats or sinks while being pulled by the line, it remains nothing but a turtle or a fish.
The fish dies; yet this is the secret art of the Tathāgata’s contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*). Even those of shallow practice and inferior faculties cannot attain it.

Seeing that my mind-nature was manifest yet outwardly light and frivolous, all people considered me utterly mad. Now, for your sake, I shall explain the method of contemplating the mind (*citta-vipaśyanā*).

One contemplates and penetrates the nature of the mind through the myriad phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*), discerning them according to their direct or reverse order, horizontal or vertical alignment, depth or shallowness, and coarseness or subtlety.
"The nature of the mind encompasses all virtues. Upon hearing these words, I conceived the perception of a Tathāgata toward that mad bhikṣu and paid him homage with a sincere heart.
When the bhikṣu finished speaking, he sat in meditation and entered samādhi; for seven days he did not rise, his body and mind remaining unmoving.
Having emerged from samādhi, his complexion was fresh and white, like the appearance of a white lotus suddenly blooming. Who would dare [disparage] such a rare occurrence?
Reflecting on this, one realizes that the mental dharmas are difficult to fathom. Those who seek the Buddha-way should simply practice the contemplation of the mind.
Judging by this, how could one possibly give rise to slander against monks who appear to be acting like madmen?
"O Bhikṣu who constantly composes poetry, you should also hear this:

As I was traveling through this country to visit the wise, some tens of *li* to the north of Mount Wutai, there is a mountain village. Within that village, on the mountainside, there were two bhikṣus who had constructed thatched huts and lived in separate dwellings.
Originally, they were both men of literary talent from Hangzhou; having shaved their heads and renounced the household life, they traveled far..."
He dwelt on this mountain, observing their activities; they did not pursue the traces of the Path nor did they abandon worldly occupations. What they delighted in were poetry and song:

fresh flowers and fragrant breezes in the morning, the bright moon illuminating the night, dipping the brush to compose verses when the cool wind blew at dusk, and raising a fan to chant hymns as the frosty cranes cried at dawn.
Beyond these, they practiced nothing else. Those of the time who saw them departed [in wonder].

The householders and non-Buddhists slandered and reviled them, yet they were not counted among the ranks of the Saṃgha. After the two bhikṣus entered the mountains, they did not emerge into the human world;
they feared neither slander nor delighted in praise. I went to visit them and saw the two monks walking out from their thatched huts;
they composed only verses and hymns, showing no trace of the spirit of the Buddha-Dharma. I stayed with them for a long time by force of effort.
He was respectful in appearance, yet his views were increasingly perverse and he would not utter a word of kindness. I never saw him practice [virtue]; I distanced myself from him and departed.
After several years had passed, I went there again. There lived two elderly monks nearby, one eighty-odd and the other ninety years of age.
At the time of their death, for a full day and night, they remained without ceasing [their practice]. Old...
They sang and chanted with flowing tears and mournful cries; upon hearing this, both monastics and laypeople considered them old madmen.

They did not recite the Buddha’s name nor read the sutras or teachings, but practiced useless and solitary worldly songs and secular texts, vainly passing their lives. These were truly great evildoers.

At that time, two elderly monks, as they approached the end of their lives, met one another at the same moment. Closing their eyes, they spoke together, held each other's hands, and wept as they chanted. At that time—
The air was filled with the sounds of celestial music, and exquisite flowers and rare fragrances pervaded the mountains and forests.

Mañjuśrī and Maitreya appeared riding upon clouds; each preached the profound and wondrous Dharma for an elderly monk. Each then escorted a monk away, ascending toward the heavens in the east and west.

A rare fragrance permeated the chamber for several months without fading. Radiant light filled the grove, shining brilliantly throughout the night. Monks, nuns, men, and women followed [in search of them].

He prostrated himself before the master’s head. After returning to his quarters and offering praises upon opening the thatched hut, he examined the poems and writings the master had composed over the years;
they were not the words of the mundane world, but were entirely the realm of the true mark (*dharmatā*) and the merit of profound contemplation of the mind.

He saw therein the reason why the impermanence of the world and the uncertainty of birth and death are non-dual with the realm of Māras and the realm of Buddhas, and the source wherein afflictions (*kleśa*) and awakening (*bodhi*) are one and the same. He beheld...

Some whose livers were stained with defilement suddenly gave rise to the mind of enlightenment; upon hearing this, others felt it to the very marrow of their bones, finding themselves unable to restrain their tears.

Some, having heard this poem, shaved their heads and entered the mountains, abandoning their kin to deeply guard the Bodhi-mind. Ashamed of their transgressions, they maintained the precepts, restraining their bodies and observing their minds.
Those who thus turned toward the Buddha-way were exceedingly numerous. Therefore, one should know that all dharmas are the Buddha-dharma; it is truly possible for one with a direct mind to attain it.
One may observe the mind; by this standard, who is the Buddha, the World-Honored One? Do not slander other sentient beings or the bhikṣus.
○ Regarding the method of bathing, the Dharma-emptiness Bhikṣu rebuked his disciples who delighted in bathing, saying:
"You bhikṣus, you clearly know the dharma of bathing for a Dharma-master. The bhikṣus replied: "We are able to know it. This is [the account].
Therefore, one should always bathe. The bhikṣu Dharmavivara again asked, "If you can know this, you may instruct me.
The disciple replied, "This is not a difficult matter. One must fully prepare the necessary implements according to the Dharma, such as water, wood, fire, a cauldron, and fragrant ashes."
He bathed in warm water that was neither hot nor cold, washing away the filth and impurities from his body;
all the people were fully aware of this. The Bhikṣu Dharmavīra said to his disciple: "What you have been practicing is not the method of bathing for a śramaṇa;
it is the bathing ritual of lay families, both men and women, practiced throughout many kalpas."

Although one bathes the body, because the defilements of black karma increase moment by moment, those who rely on such [worldly] dharmas have no means of escape from the old village of the three miserable realms;
they are merely creating the karma for the Hot Hells. How could bathing remove the filth of the body?

Though one shaves the head and dyes the robes to assume the form of a Dharma teacher, this is eternally different from the appearance of a layperson; yet one cannot know that the mind has become different simply because the outward form is different.
The layperson said, "By this I clearly know that the bathing of śramaṇas is not the same as the methods of the laity.

He continued to speak thus for my sake, while his disciple kept his mouth shut, not knowing how to respond. The bhikṣu Dharmavīra addressed his disciple, saying, "You do not yet clearly understand the mental conduct and ritual procedures of the śramaṇa’s bathing;
why then do you constantly bathe and give rise to attachment? I shall now explain the bathing for you."

Dharma. Generally, for a Dharma Master, having few desires and being content is the true practice. In the past, when our country was at its height, I traveled to a foreign land to request the Buddha-Dharma.
In that country, on a mountain to the north, there was a monastery with barely more than ten monks. In their coming and going and in their daily abiding, they all maintained the prohibitive precepts;
they would not permit a floating bag [to cross the river], fully possessed the dignified deportment, and did not spill even a drop of oil from their bowls. At that time, I arrived...

Upon arriving at that mountain temple, a bathhouse was constructed for the purpose of washing away bodily impurities. First, the superior portion [of the offerings] was presented as an offering to the resident monks.
The presiding elder (*upādhyāya*) led the assembly of monks, who arrived at the bathhouse with full dignity and decorum. Without missing their turn in the monastic order, they took their seats.

Then, burning incense and scattering flowers, they knelt with their right knees on the ground, joined their palms, and made this exhortation to the Buddhas of the ten directions: "May you bestow upon us the Bodhi..."
The assembly of noble ones, including the Bodhisattvas, bathed [the image] and made offerings, praising all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas with one voice and making this great vow:
"From this life until our final body at the ultimate end, may we always bathe the Tathāgatas, Bodhisattvas, and noble ones in this manner.
We pray that you will graciously bestow compassion to rescue and purify the defilements of body and mind for all sentient beings. Thus they made their aspiration.
"I vow to pay homage to the Triple Gem. Thereafter, at a later time, when the elder bhikṣu was about to bathe, he sat upright and composed, closed his eyes, and entered into contemplation.
He snapped his fingers several times, and from his eyes flowed tears of boundless sorrow and grief.
The other bhikṣus did likewise. At that time, I did not understand the cause and condition for this bathing; I had not yet been imbued with the Buddha-dharma, yet I witnessed this occurrence.
He joined his palms and said: "Venerable Teacher, for what reason do you snap your fingers and contemplate with such sorrowful tears, refraining from bathing?
I pray you tell me the cause; I long to hear it. The Elder Bhikṣu then replied to him:
"When you, Dharma Master, wish to bathe, you should offer the upper portion of the warm bathhouse to the Triple Gem and universally bestow it upon all beings. This is what was done above."
When it is time for the ritual bath, the resident monks must bathe according to their seniority.
If visiting monks, śrāmaṇeras, or nuns arrive from nearby areas, the resident monks shall go out to welcome them with a serene countenance, greeting them courteously without any sense of opposition.
They should cultivate a mind of reverence and respect, regarding the visitors as the Great Teacher, or as their own parents, or as those toward whom they feel the utmost affection.
In your contemplation, do not discriminate between those who are kin and those who are strangers, nor between those who are knowledgeable and those who are ignorant;
likewise, do not discriminate between men and women, or the wise and the foolish. Ensure that no one passes through here empty-handed without having bathed.
Even if you yourself have not bathed for many years, you must certainly cause visiting bhikṣus to bathe. Why is this? Because if one gives rise to [a pure mind] within the warm chamber...
With a mind of stinginess and greed, they enjoy themselves and their retinues alone, refusing to give to others, whether monastics or laypeople.
They may even revile them or cast them out. After death, they will certainly enter the Hot Hell, where their bodies are incinerated and they must swallow three hot pills.
For many kalpas, they will not know when they shall emerge. Desiring to see the retribution for their sins, they [shall see] Saṃgharakṣita and others.
In the sūtras and śāstras, it is said: "Exert yourselves! Exert yourselves! While at the *jentāka* (warm bathhouse), do not give rise to a mind of greed.

Furthermore, if any bhikṣus or other men and women possess the aspiration for the Path and desire to obtain vast benefits in both worlds, they should establish a *jentāka* to make offerings to the fourfold assembly.
According to their capacity, they should gather firewood, draw water, and provide rice gruel, beverages, undergarments, charcoal, and all other necessary items.

The requisites for bathing. Constantly harboring great compassion, one makes offerings to the Saṃgha and to all who are ill, causing them to be free from dust and defilement and also curing their diseases.
Why is this? The merit of the warm bathhouse (*jentāka*) is immeasurable and boundless.

By the power of the warm bathhouse, the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven possess bodily radiance that surpasses that of all other gods; in every birth and in every place, they remain free from the stains of affliction. Internally...

Externally bright and pure, one enters the stage of the pure Buddha-ground. For this reason, even though one’s own body has not been bathed, one should exert all one’s strength—even to the point of breaking the bones—to offer [the body] to the Sangha.
One should strictly admonish oneself against the attachment to and longing for pleasure, regarding the unbathed body as a pure body despite its impurities.
At the very moment of bathing, with a single mind of sorrowful lamentation, one should perform this contemplation: "Throughout immeasurable and incalculable kalpas..."
Come! You have come to bathe in the three hot waters that are ever-present. May those waters that wash away the impurities of my body cause me to quickly realize the stainless state of Great Bodhi.
Even if the tormentors of hell exhaust my very limbs, and even if the dust of saṃsāra increases manifold through the impurities of affliction, what would not satisfy the desire for a bath?
How much more so when one has just obtained this rare human body and fortunately encountered the Śākya [Buddha]!
In the interim of the Semblance Dharma, one may wash away the impurities of the mind with the water of the Dharma; yet how can one find delight in the hot springs of conditioned existence?

Even if one were to exhaust all effort to gather every tree and forest from the mountains and cast them into the immeasurable waters of the great ocean, bathing my body daily in a heated chamber, the four elements remain a confluence of impure essence and blood—how could the five limbs [be purified]?
When the limbs are purified, one should contemplate in this way so that no attachment arises. Furthermore, one should observe the bathhouse as being in the hells;
seeing the cauldron, one should conceive of it as being made of hot iron; seeing the boiling water, one should conceive of it as molten copper;
regarding the person drawing the water, one should conceive of them as a hell-guardian; and when entering the boat for the water, one should conceive of it as entering into intensely heated iron.

One should cultivate the perception of extreme suffering regarding the cauldron; when scrubbing the body's impurities, one should generate the perception of being cast into hell, where the wardens crush one’s limbs, tear the flesh and blood apart, and cause terror.
To bring this to rest, when lying down or sitting, one should generate the perception of lying or sitting upon a great earth of glowing iron and undergoing profound suffering.
When drinking rice gruel or broth, one should generate the perception of drinking boiling molten copper.
One should cultivate the visualization: when putting on undergarments, one should conceive of them as being made of extremely hot, blazing iron that wraps and clings to the body.

By contemplating in this way, not even a single thought of pleasure in bathing arises. Such contemplations of phenomena vary infinitely according to the breadth or narrowness of the practitioner’s wisdom.
Regarding this practice hall (*uṣṇīṣa-śālā*), there is also a method for the contemplation of the principle (*tattva*) regarding the practice hall. My own body and mind...
Do not seek a warm chamber outside; look within my own belly, for it is itself a cauldron-boat. Blood, pus, tears, and the like are the boiling water;
the three hundred and sixty bones and skeletal remains are the firewood; the warmth of my body is the flame; and the various skins of my body are the inner garments.
The sovereign mind (*citta-rāja*) is the person who bathes, while the mental factors (*caitta*) are...
This is the *karmadāna* (steward) of the sauna. In this way, the mind-king (*cittarāja*) and its mental factors (*caitta*) discipline the karma and its retribution;
they exercise mastery over bathing in the hot water of the sauna. One should truly lament the transmigration through birth and death, and furthermore, one should reflect:

pure precepts are like water, wisdom is like fire, afflictions (*kleśa*) are like firewood, and compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā*) is like a cauldron. With the water of pure precepts, one fills the cauldron of compassion.
One burns the fuel of afflictions with the fire of wisdom; through this, concentration and wisdom are brought into union.

Warm water flows forth from within the heart, and by means of this Dharma-water, one washes away the stains of beginningless deluded thoughts, the defilements of evil karma, and the dust of afflictions.
In an instant, in an instant, they are made to naturally vanish. The essence of Buddha-nature and the principle of True Suchness (tathatā) manifest subtly and wondrously from moment to moment.
Self and other are stainless; inner and outer are pure. Neither celestial Māras nor external paths can defile them, and the afflictions of birth and death no longer stain them.
To contemplate and practice in this way is true bathing. To contemplate in this way...
"This alone is the bathhouse of principle. From this day forward, you should train yourselves in this manner.
The worldly bathhouse is not a true bath; how much less so when one must face the terrifying retribution for sins in future lives?
What wise person would not follow these words? Only the deluded and ignorant fail to understand. Having spoken these words, the Elder Bhikṣu did not bathe again, but returned immediately.
"In my own quarters, the other bhikṣus likewise do not bathe. Upon hearing these words, tears involuntarily flowed from my eyes.
I have deeply resolved upon the Way and constantly aspire to bathe in the warm water of contemplating the mind. I harbor no desire for bathing in the saunas of the mundane world;
even when I have just finished bathing, I still conceive the thought that I have entered a hot hell. Therefore, you all should have faith.

"What I have taught is this: one should not be attached to bathing in a heated chamber. One should constantly contemplate impermanence and regard the bathing water of the nature of mind as that which eternally leaves behind the defilements of the mind.
When the disciple-monks heard the Great Master’s admonition, they felt deep shame and remorse;
they permanently abandoned physical bathing, sought the water of the Dharma, firmly maintained the precepts, studied the orthodox teachings, and forever set forth upon the Path.
Mind. Therefore, one should know that mind, Buddha, and sentient beings are non-different in these three respects.
One should contemplate the quiescence of the *dharmatā-tathatā* (the suchness of the nature of phenomena), for all phenomena arise from the mind in an inconceivable manner.
Regarding the practice of *nien-fo*, there was a bhikṣu named Samprajanya who addressed Prajñāmati, saying: "I am currently devoid of wisdom and lack any observance of the precepts;
I am like an ox or a sheep among men, or like a withered tree in a garden. My only activity is to recite the Buddha’s name and keep mindfulness of the Buddha as my practice.
I only pray that you, O Upādhyāya, will explain for me the meritorious qualities and mental conduct of reciting the Buddha’s name, so that I may clearly understand them."

The Upādhyāya turned toward him with a serene countenance and addressed the bhikṣu, saying: "Excellent, excellent! You are a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), for you are able to recognize the precipice of birth and death and the shore of suffering.
The Three Refuges are the primary path to Bodhi; you should practice the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*)."
Mindfulness of the Buddha is the practice for those who aspire to the higher realms. Why is this so?

Looking upward toward the void, downward toward the great earth, and sideways across the four directions—to every single place—whether among devas, humans, ghosts, animals, or other such classes of beings, all receive the compassionate skillful means of the Buddhas;
as soon as they escape suffering, they enter the city of bliss. For this reason, one should resolve to seek the Way of the Buddha.
...who, having abandoned all other activities, merely recollects the Buddhas and invokes their names.
By this merit, they cross the great ocean of the torrential flow of birth and death and realize the tranquil liberation of nirvāṇa.
I shall now explain for you the ritual for invoking the names of the Buddhas, just as I myself first gave rise to the mind of enlightenment and wandered in search of the Buddha-dharma.
Throughout various lands, he sometimes entered deep mountains to dwell upon eating grass; sometimes he stayed among burial mounds, wandering for alms;
sometimes he resided in monasteries to study and practice forever; and sometimes he mingled with villages, coming and going as he pleased.
In this manner, he spent many years visiting and studying the Buddha-dharma and seeking the Vinaya. In the kingdom of Siṃhala, there was a solitary mountain.
The peaks pierce the heavens and the valleys penetrate the depths of the earth. On Mount Gu, there is a monastery with but a single monk; it is difficult for human tracks to reach.
At that time, I climbed up and went to visit the monastery. For twenty-one days, I practiced walking meditation with diligent effort.
I observed that the conduct of this monk was truly extraordinary; he did not possess any implements such as scriptures, Dharma teachings, or ritual texts. Day by day...
Bathing with diligence during the six periods of the night, enter the hall and snap your fingers with single-minded focus. Close your eyes and contemplate, then raise your voice and chant:
"Namo to all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions. Having finished chanting this name once, contemplate for a long while.
Then, again raising your voice, say: "Namo to the Great Sage Śākyamuni Tathāgata. Contemplate for a long while, and then again recite "Śākya..."
It was exactly as before, without any difference. Thus he contemplated and invoked the name of the Buddha.

A hundred times, a thousand times, tears flowed from his eyes like a fine spring rain in early summer, or like a mountain spring. Except for the times of eating, defecating, and urinating, at all other times he remained in this state.
He offered incense, scattered flowers, and presented seasonal fruits and food as offerings according to the Dharma, while invoking the name of the Buddha.

He was known as "Closing His Eyes in Contemplation" and had no other concerns. I then reflected that this foolish monk, being ignorant, merely recites the name of the Buddha without cultivating other practices;
he is not to be associated with and should be avoided at once.
Reflecting further, I thought, "I shall now test what this bhikṣu is doing. Having formed this thought, I went to where the bhikṣu was, joined my palms, and said:
He said: "Virtuous bhikṣu, how many years have you spent dwelling in these deep mountains? For what reason do you merely recite the name of the Buddha and not cultivate other practices?
The bhikṣu listened attentively. [The deity replied: "I now clearly know the mental conduct of the bhikṣu.

You may be modest regarding my conduct and might not answer even if I were to question you for the sake of testing you; yet, out of great compassion, I wish to quell your deluded mind. You, bhikṣu..."
If a monk truly desires to seek the path to great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), he should quickly cease all thoughts of pride and inferiority toward others.

He should simply give rise to sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) and reverence for all things, and must not disparage the Buddha-dharma. Why is this? Because the Buddha-dharma is profoundly deep and cannot be known by ordinary beings.
Even a faint sound of "Namo Buddha" can accomplish all that is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) within both the mundane and supramundane realms.
This constitutes the merit of both phenomena and principle. It is like a dragon prince who, seven days after birth, can rain down sweet water to universally moisten all things;
it is also like a kalaviṅka bird within its eggshell, whose voice surpasses that of all other birds, being mournful, elegant, and subtle.
Within the single sound of the invocation "Namo Buddha," there are all the merits, wisdom, compassion,

meditative concentrations, liberations, and all roots of goodness [accumulated] by that Tathāgata from the first generation of the mind of enlightenment until the realization of the ultimate fruit, throughout the interval between them.
All are fully complete without any deficiency. Why is this? Such a combination of merits, adorned together, is called a Buddha.
The nature of the mind, its essence, its characteristics, its name, and its ritual forms are all one and no different.

It is only for the sake of transforming sentient beings that the names, essences, and characteristics manifested differ. If one seeks the fundamental nature, it is suchness, empty and quiescent. For these reasons:
When one recites the name of the Buddha, one is endowed with all merits; when one contemplates his essential nature, one likewise possesses the merits and other benefits of reciting his name.
These qualities are mutually complete and lack nothing. It is like a great net: when one mesh is pulled, all the meshes vibrate.
It is also like blended incense: when one portion is burned, the fragrance of all the perfumes wafts forth.

"Therefore, a bhikṣu need only recite the name of the Buddha and cultivate no other virtues, proceeding directly to the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), where, having shattered the armies of Māra, he realizes Great Bodhi.

Upon hearing these words, I was deeply filled with shame and remorse; I prostrated myself to seek deliverance, praying only that the Great Master would proclaim for me the method of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recollection).
The bhikṣu spoke: "There are many methods for reciting the Buddha's name."
I shall briefly explain and show you one or two phrases.

If you wish to recite the names of the Buddhas, you should place an image of the Buddha upon a pure ground, adorned according to the Dharma with banners, canopies, flowers, victory standards, exquisite blossoms, and bright lamps, exerting yourself without laziness.
Bathe in fragrant water to purify the body, rinse the mouth with willow twigs and water to cleanse away impurities, and wear clean [clothing].
One should not give rise to attachment toward clothing. One must reproach the greed, hatred, delusion, and so forth that arise from a deranged mind;
one must subdue each of these delusive afflictions one by one, ensuring they do not arise. Nevertheless, one should give rise to great compassion and make a solemn vow:
"I and all sentient beings are confused by ignorance; we do not know the characteristics of right and wrong among all phenomena, nor do we know True Suchness (*tathatā*)."
The Dharma of the quiescent true reality [is such that] one dies here and is born there in an endless cycle of transmigration. One undergoes good and evil bodies for kalpas without end;
though one feels shame for this suffering, one knows no way of escape. Like a bird with broken wings, it has no means to fly upward;

like a blind person, there is no way to perceive forms. The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have given rise to the vow of great compassion, which is able to eliminate the darkness of delusion through wisdom.

The sun’s radiance clearly illumines all sentient beings, causing them to give rise to wisdom and understanding. For this reason, I now merely invoke the names of the Buddhas and contemplate their merits.

Through the vows of the Buddhas, the eye of wisdom is awakened; reaching back to the beginningless limits of birth and death, it shines brightly upon the Dharma-realm, spontaneously and without obstruction.
Reflecting thus, I single-mindedly invoke the names of all Buddhas. Furthermore...

Contemplate that it is rare to hear the names of the Buddhas; yet, if one merely hears them, the afflictions and evil karma of immeasurable kalpas are eliminated, and one will always be born in the happy realms.
No demons or non-Buddhists can disturb such a person. It is like a wondrous medicine:
merely hearing its name extends one’s long life by three hundred years. It is also like a king of mantras: as soon as it is heard...
Poisonous and malevolent vapors will naturally be extinguished; how much more so when one single-mindedly recites the Buddha’s name, for the benefits of his merit are immeasurable and boundless.
Therefore, I now eliminate all distracted thoughts and single-mindedly recite his name.
Thus reflecting as I recite the Buddha’s name, I further contemplate the Tathāgata’s wondrous marks, which are profoundly deep and subtle, and exhaustively describe his sublime conduct.
They practice cultivation throughout kalpas, which means they vow to make the four great universal vows. They relinquish the wealth of the dharma-realm as alms to all sentient beings:
seeking eyes, they give eyes; seeking ears, they give ears; seeking hands, they give hands; seeking feet, they give feet. To those who beg for bone, they give even their marrow.
Extending even to their bodies and lives, they universally bestow them upon all, throughout the entire dharma-realm across immeasurable kalpas.

Practicing such giving with a mind free from weariness or detachment, one does not give rise to conceptualizations during that interval—such as the distinctions between the giver, the recipient, and the gift.
From ethical discipline and diligence up to wisdom, these pervade the entire *dharmadhātu*.

Throughout immeasurable eons, one does not give rise to conceptualizations, practicing as previously described in terms of giving. By thus cultivating these practices for oneself and transforming others, immeasurable merit is realized.
The subtle and wondrous body of self-enjoyment is perfectly round and boundless, with marks and signs of merit such that the mark of the invisible crown of the head pervades the entire *dharmadhātu*.
The white tuft of hair between the eyebrows likewise pervades the *dharmadhātu*.
Even down to every faculty, mark, sign, limb, and pore, each is infinite and limitless, for they are produced by the power of roots of goodness. Thus, the physical body and wisdom are [tenfold].
The powers, fearlessnesses, compassion, supernatural penetrations, samādhis, and factors of the path all pervade the dharma-realm without confusion.
They abide in mutual harmony, experiencing the bliss of the Dharma in profound stillness and tranquility. How much more so when they give rise to great compassion and recall their original vows;

out of pity for sentient beings, they manifest transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) and conceal their sublime, exalted bodies (*vairocanakāya*) to dwell in lands of segmented existence, their physical forms possessing vast dimensions.

There are minor distinctions. Among men, there are myriad differences—pure and defiled, ordinary and noble—and the physical marks, secondary characteristics, and merits of their manifested bodies are likewise inconceivable.
Such as the blue-lotus eyes with dark-blue eyelashes, the snow-mountain white teeth, the gait of a bull-king, the kalaviṅka voice, and the lion-like chest;
each of these marks and secondary characteristics is not a negative dharma, but consists of immeasurable merit.
Through this harmonious union, one focuses the mind in contemplation and raises the voice to invoke the Name. All sufferings are extinguished, and one certainly attains peace and happiness.

"May I be just like all the Buddhas; may I attain a body endowed with the marks and signs of merit, acting as a great refuge for all sentient beings, and carrying both myself and others directly to Bodhi.
Contemplating thus, one invokes the Name with single-minded devotion.
He further reflected: "The names of the Buddhas are endowed with immeasurable virtues.

If one hears the name of a Buddha while in the hells, the fierce fires are extinguished and transformed into lotus ponds. If one hears the Buddha’s name while among the hungry ghosts, the nectar of immortality appears before them and the suffering of hunger is eliminated.
For asuras, humans, and devas, each according to their respective capacity, it may remove fear, poverty, or the five signs of decay."
It gives rise to all wholesome dharmas; it brings peace and happiness in this life and the realization of the fruit in the future.

Such benefits are naturally and fully possessed at the very moment one calls upon the Buddha's name with single-mindedness. Therefore, call upon the Buddha’s name with a focused mind, and further contemplate how the skillful means of the Buddhas are profoundly deep and subtle.
Should there be sentient beings who call upon his name with single-mindedness, his unimpeded wisdom will naturally know them.
Seeing [the practitioner] arrive at his place, he extends his hand of compassion to stroke their crown and protect them.
He teaches and guides them, increasing wholesome dharmas and diminishing unwholesome dharmas. Gradually teaching and transforming them, he leads them into the Buddha-way.
This benefit is like the pure, full moon naturally floating upon the water, or like a peahen conceiving by relying on the sound of thunder. Such are the benefits.
Single-mindedly recite the Name, further reflecting that one’s life has already passed away like water flowing down a mountain;
that one’s physical life suddenly declines like a hibiscus flower; that sinful karma has accumulated within the body and afflictions fill the mind;

and that at the time of death, one is oppressed by various illnesses and disturbed by manifold sufferings, with the faculties scattered and the physical form wasting away, as the messengers of Yama question and determine one’s offenses.
Regarding the signs of the gravity of one’s karma: ox-headed and horse-headed beings surround them from front and back, crushing and breaking their limbs;
malevolent ghosts and spirits, watching for vulnerabilities both inside and out, redouble their suffering and affliction. Their beloved wives and children shed tears and lose all sense of direction;
their dependents and kin harbor grief and sorrow. Friends and old acquaintances, seeing their countenance, do not come to visit. Those who were close...
Neighbors hear of one’s misfortunes within their own courtyards, yet they do not inquire after them; royal law presses down upon wives and children from above, while grief rises from below.
Wealth accumulated over a lifetime departs in all four directions; though one adorns the body morning and evening, it is entirely decayed and diminished.
At that critical moment, who can provide rescue or compassionate protection? The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, extend the power of great compassion and manifest before one. With loving-kindness...

With a body of compassionate radiance and gentle speech, he beckons and welcomes them upon a lotus pedestal. All heavy sufferings are extinguished as they are born into the Pure Land, where they behold the Buddha and hear the Dharma.
Such benefits are truly rare. Reflecting thus, one should single-mindedly recollect the Buddha.
Furthermore, reflect that to recite the name of the single Buddha Amitābha is to recite the names of all Buddhas. For what reason?

Because the Tathāgatas of the three bodies share the same essence, the same intention, and the same activities as all Buddhas, all Buddhas are endowed with the fruits of the merits of the three bodies.
Therefore, by reciting the name of the single Buddha Amitābha, one universally accomplishes the recitation of the names of all Buddhas.
Contemplating in this way, one should practice mindfulness of the Buddha with a single mind. Such is the matter of the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha through reciting his name.
Buddha-recollection (*buddhānusmṛti*) has infinite aspects; however, one should contemplate each according to the breadth or narrowness of the practitioner’s wisdom.

If one wishes to directly recollect the merits of the Buddhas, one should contemplate the principle of reality (*tattva*). There are three types of contemplation of the principle of reality in Buddha-recollection:

first, one should directly contemplate that one's own body is itself the physical form of the Tathāgata; second, one should directly contemplate that one's own mind is itself the [mind] of the Tathāgata.

Regarding the nature of the mind: one should directly contemplate that mountains, rivers, grasses, trees, and even a single speck of dust are themselves the subtle and wondrous body and mind of the Tathāgata.
First, as for directly contemplating the body as the Buddha-body: one contemplates all parts of one’s own body—the head, eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and even the hands and feet.
Although these may at first appear to be the impermanent body of birth and death, upon further investigation and contemplation, one realizes they are fully endowed [with the Buddha-nature].
The body of form, which is the perfected merit of boundless reality, is eternally pervasive; its continuity is serene, being neither existent nor non-existent.
The head is itself emptiness, and emptiness is itself the head. It is the same for all parts of the body, such as the eyes, ears, and nose.

In profound union with True Suchness (*tathatā*), it transcends the path of verbal discourse and exceeds the realm of conceptual thought. Thus, my own body is the purity of the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*).
The pure Dharma-body is apart from this body of mine; where else could one seek the Dharma-body?

Each and every part of the Tathāgata’s body pervades the entire Dharma-realm without any further confusion. It is only due to deluded attachment that one discriminates between right and wrong, or between breadth and narrowness.
If one examines its fundamental nature, every single pore of the body parts, such as the head and so forth, is identical to the Dharma-realm, sovereign and unimpeded.
Is it not the case that the merits of the marks and embellishments of the Reward Body are fully present within my own body? How much more so is the Response Body itself my very own body?
Now, when I observe my own body, it is no different from that of the Buddha. The crown of my head is the Tathāgata’s mark of the invisible summit.
My hair and body hairs are the deep blue-black hair-mark of all Buddhas.
When I observe my two eyes, they are the World-Honored One’s eyes of great compassion, as fresh and white as a blue lotus. As for my voice, is it not the eightfold [melody] of the kalaviṅka?
Regarding the characteristics of his voice: lips like the *bimba* fruit are present within my mouth;
a lion’s chest is my own chest; skin the color of purple gold is my own body-skin; and the thousand-spoked wheel mark is complete upon the soles of my feet.
The lotus flowers upon which the Tathāgata treads when walking are the very things I step upon as I walk. As for the superior robes and Dharma-garments worn by the Tathāgata—
As well as various necklaces and ornaments—these are the garments and finery worn upon my body, these are the accoutrements that adorn it.

When I observe my body as a whole, it is no different from that of the Buddha. Because of the power of cultivation, one is freed from evil karma; thus, the marks and signs of a Tathāgata appear with brilliant clarity.

Being free from defilement and radiantly pure, they are a joy for all to behold. Because of the power of deluded thoughts, one creates manifold karmas; thus, the bodies of sentient beings [are otherwise].
The primary and secondary marks are obscured; shrouded by dust and defilements, they are sullied and lusterless, abandoned by all.
Yet when one contemplates their fundamental nature, there is only oneness without difference. It is like gold that has been refined and emits light, yet remains hidden within dark earth;

or like the surface of a mirror that is polished until it is brilliant and clear, yet becomes dim when covered with accumulated dust. For this reason, one should contemplate that the primary and secondary marks of my body are no different from one's own.

The enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and the other-enjoyment body (*parasaṃbhogakāya*) are equal and without distinction in their marks and signs (*lakṣaṇavyañjana*). One should merely repent of the causes and conditions of deluded thoughts and inversions;
quickly recollect the merits of the Buddhas of the past, and recollect that one’s own body is inherently endowed with the Buddha-body.
Thus, dwelling in tranquility within original enlightenment (*mūlapratyavekṣā*), one should contemplate and recite the Buddha’s name in this way. Second, contemplate that one’s own mind is...
As for the Buddha-mind: the mind and intention of all Buddhas are precisely my own mind and intention. Within my own mind, I observe the three seeds of Buddhahood and the seeds of the five wisdoms.
That which the Buddhas of the three periods of time have cultivated is called True Suchness (*tathatā*), known as the Dharma-realm body (*dharmadhātu-kāya*) and the Dharma-realm mind.

All skillful means are fully complete therein, without any deficiency. Because the Dharma-body is omnipresent, the Reward-body (*saṃbhoga-kāya*) and the Transformation-body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*) are likewise omnipresent throughout the Dharma-realm.
The realms, as well as the primary causes, conditions, and wisdom, are likewise all-pervasive. When observing in this way, one’s own body, all Buddhas, and all sentient beings are entirely equal;
thus, one should recite their names and contemplate their essential nature. To contemplate in this manner is what is called "true mindfulness of the Buddha.
Third, one contemplates that grasses, trees, and all things are themselves the Buddha. Why? Because the Buddha-nature is like space and is all-pervasive.
Regarding all things, how can one proclaim a distinction between the existence or non-existence of sentient and insentient beings?

Therefore, one should contemplate that all insentient things are also the Buddhas. A single form and a single fragrance are purely the Middle Way; a single sound and a single flavor are likewise True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Whether moving or still, they are the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*); whether coarse or subtle, they are entirely the Reality-mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Reality...
The realm of the myriad dharmas, wherein wisdom dwells, is itself the Dharmakāya. For this reason, one should contemplate that even insentient things are all the Dharmakāya.
It is because those of such a kind lack the eye of wisdom that they perceive only grasses, trees, tiles, stones, and other such objects.
It is neither Buddha-nature nor the Buddha-body; it is merely called an insentient, decayed object.
This is inconceivable, known clearly only by the Buddhas. It is not within the realm of ordinary people with shallow understanding.
For this reason, do not debate this matter, but simply look up to it with faith and acceptance, lest those things such as grasses, trees, tiles, and stones should see [it otherwise].

We sentient beings all give rise to this thought: "Since we—beings such as grasses, trees, tiles, and stones—all possess the principle of the Buddha-nature within the *dharmadhātu*, it stands to reason that we naturally become Buddhas, radiate light, and preach the Dharma.
By what causes and conditions do all sentient beings of the womb-born, egg-born, moisture-born, and transformation-born classes attain Buddhahood? This is inconceivable; who [could know it]?"
To know the fundamental cause: it is due to deluded thoughts that one experiences these myriad distinctions—grass, trees, tiles, stones, gold, jade, fragrance, stench, good, and evil.

Being confused and ignorant, one fails to recognize that the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is eternally abiding and not insentient. Both ourselves and those sentient beings each possess the merit of Buddha-nature;
this is the fundamental cause for becoming a Buddha. Such is the source of our strange doubts, just as with us.

When these people heard what the Buddha had taught—that the Buddha-nature pervades even insentient things such as grasses and trees—they all gave rise to strange thoughts, yet they clung to their own views and would not change their minds.
They asked, "By what causes and conditions are all dharmas so inconceivable? Aside from the World-Honored Buddha, there is no one who can realize and know them."
Inanimate and animate things are originally of the nature of the Dharma; how much more so when the Sūtra says:

"When one Buddha attains Buddhahood, he perceives that all grasses and trees throughout the entire Dharma-realm are universally the body of the Buddha—six feet tall, emitting light and preaching the Dharma—and each such Buddha is named the Tathāgata Sublime Enlightenment.

The Sangha dwells therein, all of them upholding the prohibitive precepts without transgressing even a speck of dust. At mealtime, they carry their alms bowls into the villages to beg for food;

Among them was one who constantly delighted in fine dwellings. He constructed houses from precious timber and plastered the foundations with various colors.
After begging for alms, he would devote himself solely to the business of building houses; having finished one, he would demolish it, and having demolished it, he would build another again.
When I saw this at that time, I sighed deeply in great astonishment. The other monks declared, "This is the monk’s unprofitable occupation."
He had been residing in his quarters for over thirty years. Seeing that his age was advanced and his strength failing, we constantly exhorted him, saying:

Thus, thus shall I humble myself. Moment by moment, I lament that my life has reached its twilight. Thus he spoke, gathering [the assembly].
The entire assembly was moved to resolve their minds upon the unsurpassed path to enlightenment. Thereafter, he preached for them the Dharma-gate of the Direct Mind.
"The mind is the land; the mind is bodhi. By contemplating my single mind, one knows all dharmas; by reflecting on my single mind, one beholds all Buddhas.
To give rise to a single thought-moment is to pass through immeasurable kalpas; even after incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, one has not transcended that single thought-moment. It is like a dream."
The moment prior to awakening after a thousand years within is when one has not yet attained true enlightenment and remains constantly in a dream;

The wise, like the Honored One Śākyamuni, now regard your body as one would pick up a spat-out morsel of spittle. You must quickly observe the mind and not allow it to become heedless.

Regarding the distinctions: one should contemplate the quiescence of the *dharmatā-tathatā* (the suchness of the nature of phenomena), for all phenomena are inconceivable.
As for the contemplation of the Buddha’s thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*), Master Baozhi said:

Why is this? I recall that in the past I went to the land of Hu.

His mouth did not utter a sound and his body took no step. In his dwelling, there were no other miscellaneous utensils or belongings. If anyone gave him food, he would [accept it]...

I experienced something extraordinary, yet it was distinct from what I had previously completed. At the onset of the first watch of the night, I went again to see the Saṃgha.

As before, there was a sixteen-foot Tathāgata emitting radiance, his marks and signs subtle and wondrous, sitting in tranquil composure. I prostrated deeply and gazed upon him throughout the entire night without seeing any change in his appearance.

One night, while I was staying there, I saw a bhikṣu constantly contemplating the form of the Tathāgata.

Within my heart, I seek nothing further outward. I believe his teaching; for many years I have long contemplated the Tathāgata’s marks and signs, his compassion, and his great vows within my own mind.
From this point onward, there is no other practice beyond this. Hearing the monk’s words, I have deeply awakened the aspiration for the Way.
How clear it is! The mind is replete with all virtues; who would seek Bodhi if they do not contemplate the mind? Therefore—

○ On the southern coast, there were two bhikṣus whose story was told as follows:

"I recall that in the past, while seeking the traces of the Way and searching for virtuous friends, I saw on the shore of the southern sea two bhikṣus. Although their forms resembled those of monks, they were like fishermen."
They set out boats and nets to catch fish every day; regardless of whether it was windy or rainy, they did nothing but this, having no other occupation.
When I saw this, unwholesome thoughts arose within me toward those monks: "In the ocean of the Vinaya, they leave behind no remains;
in the garden of the Dharma King, they uproot poisonous trees. For what offense do I see these monks so loathsome?"
I stayed for one night near the boundary. That night, I dreamed of a śramaṇa of dignified and composed demeanor who held an incense burner and paid homage to a fisherman-monk.
He then came to me and rebuked me, saying: "Why have you conceived a mind of slander toward a noble one?
Your retribution in future lives will be as described in the sūtras. You should go at once to that noble one and offer repentance. Upon waking from the dream, [I reflected].

Later, his body and mind were filled with heat and distress. Waiting for the sun to rise, he ran to where the two bhikṣus who were fishermen were, prostrated himself before them in reverence, and related his thoughts.
He confessed his slander of the Great Teacher and requested the compassionate means to extinguish his transgressions.
The two fishermen replied, "Excellent! Son of the Śramaṇa’s Dharma, who would possess such wisdom?"

Such a person brings forth slander toward the myriad dharmas. Why is this? For mountains, rivers, grasses, and trees—whether sentient or insentient—all were formerly my own bodies and all were my parents.
Even while wandering through delusion, they still possess such kindness; how much more so when one seeks their fundamental nature, for they are all True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Within True Suchness, there is neither enemy nor kin, neither sentient nor insentient; yet [this person] slanders and praises.
They praise the pure and the impure. Therefore, the wise person perceives all phenomena as the marks of a Buddha and does not deceive any phenomenon;
thus, repentance is the great principle. However, we are of evil discipline, sustaining our lives by capturing and killing sentient beings;
when our bodies perish and our lives end, we shall return to the evil realms. Therefore, virtuous people distance themselves from us.
...and so forth. They spoke these words: "We boarded a boat and took our nets out to the great ocean.
At that time, I deeply observed the conduct of the bhikṣus and stayed near them for several days. Day and night, I inquired after them and sought the causes and conditions for awakening.
The two bhikṣu-saṃghas said to me: 'The two of us were originally fishermen; having left home to enter the Way, we have nothing further [to do with our former lives].'"
I know this. Through what I have previously practiced in seeking the Buddha-way, I contemplate that my own mind-nature is the Dharma-nature;
it is the Buddhas, it is compassion, and it is wisdom. With great vows, I shall deliver all sentient beings and establish them on the other shore.
Thus, one contemplates the boat and the net as the object of focus. Why is this so? The mind of compassion is the very essence of the boat.

One adorns this boat with the practice of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*). The perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) is that upon which the ten thousand practices depend, just as the hull of a boat is that upon which all its cargo depends.
The perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) prevents what is wrong and stops evil, just as the planks along the sides of a boat shield it from people and objects.
It prevents one from falling into the water. The practice of patience nurtures and covers all other practices, just as the cabin roof of a ship covers the goods within.
The merit of diligence leads swiftly to the fruit of Buddhahood, just as the oars of a ship must be moved by intent for it to proceed.

The perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*) subdues distraction and establishes stability, just as a ship that does not leak remains secure and steady. Wisdom is like a skilled helmsman who can discern the way.
Selection. It is like a boatman who skillfully fans the river current and so forth. In this way, one adorns the vessel of the great vow.

The Bodhisattva of Great Compassion boards this ship and, using the net of the scriptural teachings, drags across the ocean of birth and death to rescue the fish and turtles of sentient beings drowning in the mud of saṃsāra, establishing them in the secret treasury of nirvāṇa. Such conduct is the work of a Buddha. As it is said:
"This is the practice of Bodhisattvas. We have trained in such compassionate vows, sailing by boat day after day and roaming the ocean night after night.
Since we left the household life, we have not committed even a minor offense, let alone the act of catching fish to sustain our lives.
This is merely a skillful means that is easy to recognize through contemplative practice, and it is also that which has been cultivated through great compassion. Having spoken thus, [the two]—2.

instead, there were Tathāgatas sitting upon lotuses, their number being immeasurable.

Their bodies were each one chi or perhaps one chi tall, emitting radiant light and each manifesting supernatural transformations. The bhikṣus prostrated themselves and praised them with all their hearts. No...
