The merit of observing the dharma-realm of the mind is such that you must not let others of little wisdom hear of it; otherwise, they will lose the benefit of both worlds.
You should keep this hidden within your heart and observe the nature of the mind. Having heard and seen this, my joy redoubled, and I made a vow.
With a bodhicitta, observe the mind even more closely. You should examine this matter: seeing a monk who has broken the precepts, how could you give rise to slander?
○ The bhikṣu Udraka asked another bhikṣu, "What is the practice of that bhikṣu?
The bhikṣu replied, "I now simply pay homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions; throughout the day and night, I prostrate to the Buddha a thousand times. Udraka...
The Buddha spoke to the bhikṣus: "What the śramaṇas practice is a most difficult task; to be able to perform a thousand prostrations day and night without retreating is truly arduous.
I now rejoice in the practice of these bhikṣus. For my sake, explain the method for worshipping the Buddha so that it may also be practiced with diligence.
The bhikṣus replied: "There is no formal ritual; one simply stands before the Buddha, vocally reciting 'Namo' [Homage], and joins the two hands."
Placing one’s palms together and bowing the head to the Buddha constitutes the ritual form. The bhikṣu Udraka said to the bhikṣu, “What you have spoken concerns external appearances and deportment;
what I now ask concerns that which is contemplated within the mind. With what mental state do you pay homage and respect to the Buddhas?
The bhikṣu replied, “I have no further thoughts; I merely hear the cause for obtaining merit. For some years he has been performing this prostration.

The Buddha, knowing the thoughts within the mind of the bhikṣu Udraka, said to him: "Bhikṣu, I shall explain for you the method of prostration, so that you may understand its profound and deep sphere of merit.
Bhikṣu, listen attentively! In the final age, sentient beings will barely give rise to a wholesome mind;

though they diligently practice the Buddha-dharma, they will not seek out its profound meaning. They will not know right from wrong, nor the internal and external rules of decorum, nor the characteristics of the mind."
Their mindfulness is entirely lost and confused; though they pay homage to the Triple Gem, they do not maintain outward decorum, and their inner minds are not in accord.
They are like a drunkard who is unaware of rising or lying down, or like a pestle that moves up and down according to the foot’s motion.

Such prostrations are not called "paying homage to the Buddha," and the merit obtained is exceedingly meager. If one pays homage in accordance with the Dharma, the roots of goodness produced are inconceivable.

As for the measure [of this]: it is like the vows of Samantabhadra and others in worshipping the Buddhas, and also like the mind of the nature of the Buddha in the worship of the Unconquerable One (Adhimātra).

Worshiping the Buddha in such a manner is called true worship of the Buddha. I recall that in the past, disregarding my own body and life and paying no heed to food or clothing, I traveled throughout the five regions of India in search of the Buddha-Dharma.
In the kingdom of Saṃghāta, there was a Dharma Master named Śraddhaguṇa; at that time, I went to him.
I went to where that Dharma Master was and asked him: "What fault is there in merely prostrating to the Buddhas without generating mental contemplation at the time of worship?

As for someone as ignorant as I, I do not even understand the shallow; how much less could I understand the profound contemplation of the mind? I have heard that the Buddhas possess all manner of merit and virtue;
therefore, although I do not contemplate, by simply performing prostrations, my merit should be profound. It is like sweet food, which remains so even if one does not perceive it."
One knows the sweet and bitter tastes; yet when food enters the belly, it merely serves to enhance one's complexion and sustain life.

By this analogy, one should know that even if one understands the ritual procedures for preparing sweet food, if one does not eat it when it enters [the mouth], it cannot benefit the body. Likewise, although one may perform mental contemplations, if one does not pay homage to the Buddha, one will not obtain benefit.
Conversely, although one may not perform such contemplations, if one simply practices paying homage to the Buddha, one will certainly become a Buddha. Sweet food is like this.
The Buddha, having partaken of his meal according to the ritual, understood the nature of the food through the practice of contemplation and replied: "Listen attentively.

From the time I was young until I reached old age, I have examined the Buddha's teachings; I have never heard it said that one seeking Bodhi does not employ contemplative observation and instead cultivates virtue with a distracted mind.
Rather, I have only heard it taught that one should cultivate all activities by means of contemplation. Have you not heard this stated in the various sutras?"

The contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) cures the disease of desire for food, as do the contemplation of counting the breath (*ānāpāna-smṛti*), the contemplation of the elements (*dhātu-prakāra*), the contemplation of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), the contemplation of great compassion (*mahāmaitrī-karuṇā*), the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*), the contemplation of the four roots of goodness (*catvāri kuśalamūlāni*), the contemplation of the sixteen aspects (*ṣoḍaśākāra*), the contemplation of the sixteen emptinesses (*ṣoḍaśa-śūnyatā*), and the contemplation of the sixteen characteristics (*ṣoḍaśa-lakṣaṇa*).
Thus, there are immeasurable methods of contemplation, ranging up to the contemplation of the single reality (*eka-tattva-bhāvanā*) and others; their number is infinite.
What is called "contemplation" (vipaśyanā) is precisely the contemplation of the mind. If there is no contemplation, these dharmas cannot be accomplished.

Furthermore, have you not heard that the five pāramitās and all other practices are like the blind and the lame? The single dharma of Prajñā is like one who has eyes, and is also like hands and feet capable of leading the blind and the lame.
Thus, the five perfections and myriad virtues are safely protected and guided toward the Buddha-bodhi.

That which is called *prajñā* (wisdom) is likewise the contemplation of the mind. From this, one should know that if one practices virtue with a distracted mind lacking contemplation, one cannot sever the afflictions (*kleśa*) nor realize the fruit of Buddhahood.
It is like a foolish person who, having turned away from all skillful means, feels joy upon obtaining a mere trifle of food;
because of the power of that food, he does not seek further sustenance, yet he still sets aside a great tally to calculate the affairs of the kingdom.
All the food, clothing, jade, money, elephants, horses, carriages, wives, children, kinsmen, fields, houses,

and all manner of wealth accumulated by kings, ministers, and elders— through such various experiences as these, day and night, my mind has continuously and incessantly longed for wealth and treasures,
thinking of my own poverty. Even though there are treasures in great quantity, [I have been made to] lose them moment by moment.

One’s physical strength is utterly exhausted, and there is no benefit whatsoever from even a single grain or half a coin; how much less could one obtain wealth? It would be better to exert oneself to seek further food and other necessities.
If one uses them for oneself or bestows them upon one's wife and children, their bodies and minds will find peace and happiness.
Bhikṣus, you should know that such foolish people are precisely those sentient beings caught in birth and death. Though they employ various skillful means, they only manage to obtain a small amount.

Eating. For example, by means of even a small amount of merit, one obtains the fruits of human or celestial rebirth; or by encountering the Buddha’s teaching, one attains the vehicles of the Two Vehicles (Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha).
Kings, ministers, and others are like the wealth and treasures of all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and noble sages. All manner of good deeds are like placing them upon the counting board of calculation;

yet if one practices virtue with a distracted mind, although the number is great, there is not even the benefit of half a coin. It is the same as not observing the mind—there is nothing more [to gain].

This benefit is precisely what the Tathāgata has definitively taught. Judging by this, if one does not practice the contemplation of the mind, then even though one cultivates meritorious deeds, there is truly no benefit.
The analogy of the sweet food that you previously cited also originates from the sūtras and śāstras.
You must not follow your own whims when applying the Dharma. I shall now apply the Dharma for you so that you may hear it.
Sweet food is like the fruit of Buddhahood and Bodhi; seeking sweet food is like the diligence of one who is distracted. Though one obtains it, not eating it is like not practicing contemplation.
To understand the characteristics of food is like understanding the characteristics of dharmas. Although one understands the characteristics of food, one does not consume it;

just as one understands the characteristics of conduct while practicing all Buddha-dharmas, one practices without observing whether the mind is distracted. One who does not understand the characteristics of food merely obtains its consumption.
It is like being ignorant of the myriad practices of *bahusruta* (extensive learning), yet merely practicing the cultivation of mindfulness and single-mindedly engaging in cultivation;
in this way, one may gradually come to know how to harmonize with the Dharma. If the body performs prostrations to the Buddhas while the mind is not in accord, it is not called true prostration.

When the body does not prostrate to the Buddha but the mind contemplates *tathatā* (suchness), this is called true prostration. If there is no contemplative mind, the roots of goodness one cultivates are like that withered tree.
Flowers bloom and fruit ripens. It is like a dead person who possesses no further mind or spirit.
Contemplation is the very life-force of the Buddha-dharma. Contemplation is the refuge of all phenomena. Contemplation is the dwelling place of the Dharmakāya.
Contemplation is the provision for birth and death. Contemplation is the guide to Bodhi. Contemplation is...

They are the parents of the mind of the Way. Therefore, when a practitioner performs prostrations to the Buddha, engages in recitation, or indeed performs any other activity, they must necessarily practice mindfulness and contemplation.
They should inquire after the Dharma and dwell with a sincere heart, praising it with faith and virtue, saying:
"How rare! Though the Dharma has long been in decline and the minds of sentient beings have become turbid, they still do not fail to seek the Dharma."
"Vimalakīrti, your earnest quest for this is truly rare. I possess no knowledge nor any virtue of precepts; my daily practice consists only of paying homage to the Buddha.
Having spoken these words, the Bhikṣu Śraddhāguṇa bathed himself to cleanse all impurities, both internal and external.
Fully endowed with dignified deportment, he held an incense burner in his hand and burned various famous fragrances. Having emerged from his room, he proceeded by slow degrees.
He walked forward, contemplating and observing until he reached the door of the hall. He stood there for a long while, his tears flowing as he wept in sorrow.

Before entering the hall, he was already struck with a sense of awe and fear; he felt a profound sense of reverence and humility. As soon as he entered the interior of the hall, he remained cautious and composed, never leaving the presence of the Buddha.
He contemplated with palms joined for a short time, single-mindedly beholding the Buddha. Having just left the Buddha’s presence, he circumambulated him.
After circumambulating seven times, he prostrated before the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Kneeling with palms joined, he scattered flowers and burned incense.
Facing the Buddha, he contemplated while remaining standing in worship. At each prostration, he closed his eyes and remained so for a long time. He performed one hundred prostrations until dusk.
Having finished the worship of the Buddha, he continued to contemplate, weeping with grief and longing, snapping his fingers in anxious remembrance, gradually...
Upon returning to his quarters, I saw this monk performing a most extraordinary prostration before the Buddha. A deep faith arose within me, and I said to Xinde:
"I have seen people in the world who, after prostrating before the Buddha, do not remain for long nor do they weep; they quickly finish their prostrations and leave the hall early.
For what reason does the Great Master perform such a prostration? I wish to hear the cause and conditions; I desire to listen now. The bhikṣu replied: [The rest of the text follows].
He said: "The sentient beings of the world are possessed by mad afflictions and fail to restrain their body and mind. Because the inner mind is deranged, the outer body finds no peace.
When the mind is left loose like a monkey, how can it be made to abide? Therefore, performing wholesome deeds is like dust before the wind, or like a whirling firebrand;
they leave no trace at the bottom of the heart. How, then, can one enter the secret treasury? Generally, there are two kinds of bowing to the Buddha: first, ritual bowing (*vastu-vandana*)."

The Buddha. Second is the worship of the Buddha through principle (*li*). Beyond these two types, how can one perform the worship of the Buddha’s radiance? Regarding the worship of the Buddha through phenomena (*shi*):

internally harboring a sense of shame and remorse is called internal purity; externally sweeping away dust and filth so that negligence does not manifest, while generating deep respect, is called external purity.
Proceeding from one's chamber to the hall, one reflects and observes: "From beginningless time until this day, I have been caged..."
Dwelling in the house of fire, one does not know how to exit the door. Now, following the Buddha’s teaching, one emerges from the burning house and proceeds toward the Pure Land.
Every step taken is no longer a step within saṃsāra; with every footfall, one reaches the Pool of Cool Refreshment. Reflecting thus, one gradually approaches the hall door.
Yet, though one exerts all heart and mind in devotion, one cannot enter prematurely. Those who seek my own body find only the three poisons and the four snakes—dust and defilement.
It is filled with the defilements of toil and entangled by them; it is unfit for association, like excrement and urine, or like mud and filth.
Yet, with such a body, one suddenly gains entry into the hall. Now, that which is called the "hall" is the ground of purity, accomplished through all manner of goodness and entirely devoid of evil.
Buddhas and Bodhisattvas constantly come to dwell therein; it is luminous and pure both inside and out. Even if there were impurities, [the hall would remain so].
"It is defiled and impure. The benevolent deities who protect the Dharma have all swept and cleansed it. How can my impure body enter here? Thinking thus, he was filled with deep fear.
He felt shame and remorse, grieving over his impurity; weeping and trembling with apprehension, he entered through the power of faith.
As soon as he had entered the hall, he thought only of having entered the chamber of compassion. Toward the Buddhas, he conceived a profound sense of respect and reverence.
Regarding the thought of encountering [the Buddha]: for immeasurable kalpas one may not hear the name of a Buddha, but instead encounter evil friends who increase the cycle of birth and death.

It is rare indeed to encounter the honored image of a Tathāgata. Now, with all my heart, I pay homage to all Buddhas, observing one by one the Tathāgata’s merits—the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics—and the causes and conditions of his adornment with myriad virtues.

With a mind of sympathetic joy, one performs a profound prostration. Such contemplation is called the ritual of worshipping the Buddha through phenomena (*nāma-vastu*). As for the ritual of worshipping the Buddha through principle (*tattva*):
my own mind is the hall; the sovereign mind (*citta-rāja*) is the Buddha; and the mental factors (*caitasika*) are the retinue of samādhi-dharmas.
When the single mind moves, the three bodies (*trikāya*) move; when the single mind abides, the three bodies abide. To worship one Buddha is to worship all Buddhas. Thus one worships.
To pay homage to all Buddhas is to pay homage to one Buddha; if one pays homage to all Buddhas, one pays homage to my own mind.
If one pays homage to my own mind, one pays homage to all Buddhas. To contemplate the single mind is to see all Buddhas; to contemplate all Buddhas is to see the single mind.
It is both the single mind and all Buddhas, yet it is neither the single mind nor all Buddhas. These arise due to deluded attachment.
"Buddha" and "non-Buddha"—this is a seeking based on differentiation. In their fundamental source, all things are as suchness (*tathatā*);

the nature and characteristics of both the one who prostrates and the object of prostration are empty and quiescent. It is like a phantom person prostrating to a phantom person, or like space prostrating to space.
Although it is inconceivable, there is still response and resonance; all Buddhas manifest within my own mind, just as a clear mirror can reflect [images].
All phenomena are like the bright moon dwelling within all waters. Contemplating in this way, one pays homage to all Buddhas;
then, all Buddhas naturally manifest. This is called inconceivable homage, and it is also called true homage, equal homage, and complete homage.
Within a single act of homage, all Buddha-dharmas are definitively and perfectly fulfilled, appearing as they truly are.
It is not lacking. I have now faithfully accepted and practiced such prostrations for six years.
During a single prostration, I saw a transformed Buddha with his hand reaching out to stroke my head, praising me, saying, "Excellent! You should prostrate to all Buddhas as I do.
Within a single prostration, I beheld the True Buddha. Hearing these words, my heart was filled with joy, like a person who, in the midst of extreme thirst, obtains [water].
This is the sublime nectar. One who upholds this Dharma should, at the time of prostrating to the Buddha, give rise to this contemplation:
"O Bhikṣu-saṃgha, follow my words; prostrate to the Buddha according to the Dharma so that you may swiftly eliminate afflictions and realize great enlightenment.

Upon hearing this, the bhikṣus raised their voices and wept bitterly: "We no longer know the method for prostrating to the Buddha. We have performed empty, useless, and shameless prostrations until now. Now..."
From this day forward, following the instructions of the Great Master, one should cultivate such contemplation at the time of prostrating to the Buddha.

A bhikṣu, taking faith as the basis, should cultivate the contemplation of phenomena according to their principles and give reverent homage to the Triple Gem. At the time of death, a transformation Buddha will come to welcome and lead them toward the Western Land.

If one wishes to enter the hall to prostrate to the Buddha, one must perform the ritual according to this method of contemplative practice. Therefore, one should know that it is the mind [that matters].

The Buddha, sentient beings, and the three [realms] are without distinction. One should contemplate the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) as quiescent, for all phenomena arise from the mind in an inconceivable manner.
Master Zhiguang had several disciples. Among them was one disciple who constantly delighted in eating much. Just as...
Just as it is the worldly custom to eat two meals each day, morning and evening, Jñānaprabha said to his disciples, "How is it that food tastes sweet and benefits the body?
Can you know this? Explain it to me. The disciples replied, "This is not a difficult matter.

When rice, oil, salt, and ginger are mixed together to season the food, and one eats until the belly is full, the vital energy becomes abundant and the flesh of the body grows plump and flourishing. However, if one eats coarse food..."

It is evil. One’s strength diminishes and it benefits the body very little. Therefore, the Great Master always preferred flavorful food, so that his five limbs and bodily flesh might be nourished and made plump.
As the Dharma Master Zhiguang was about to ordain a disciple, he snapped his fingers, looked toward the heavens, wept with grief, and said to his disciples:
"You must not utter such evil words. Upon hearing these words, my body and mind were [distressed]."

"Ānanda, what you have previously said regarding methods of eating is not the teaching of the Buddha, nor is it the practice of a śramaṇa; rather, it is the teaching of the evil discipline of non-Buddhists.
Those who follow your instructions and constantly indulge in fine food will surely fall into the three miserable realms and the states of no leisure.
I shall now explain the proper method for eating."
In the past, when I was staying under a tree in the kingdom of Saṃkassa, there was an elderly monk who came to that tree while wandering for alms with his bowl.
He held up his bowl and prostrated several times, then sat down in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*).

He divided the food in his bowl into seven portions—six equal parts and one slightly smaller—and after making a single prostration to each of the four portions of rice, he reflected and contemplated them individually.
He set it aside and divided the remainder into two portions, giving one portion to me and one portion to a dog that was staying nearby, while using the remaining small portion for his own food.
When the bhikṣu had finished distributing the portions, as he was about to eat, his body and mind remained unmoving; with eyes closed, he entered contemplation.
After a short time, he raised his hand and snapped his fingers, then cried out loudly. As soon as he finished crying and laughing, he opened [his eyes].
Upon seeing the food with his eyes, he conceived a sense of dread; his body trembled and he wept even more bitterly. He would not eat the rice at all.
Having given his own portion of food to a dog, he took four portions of food and either cast them into the river or placed them in the forest, never eating it himself.
He washed his alms-bowl and departed. I saw this rare conduct of the bhikṣu and followed behind him as he went.
That bhikṣu went to a cemetery and sat with his body upright. I paid homage to the bhikṣu and addressed him with a sincere heart:
"Great Master, for what reason do you not eat today? You have given alms to all and returned with your bowl washed. Furthermore, for what cause and condition do you weep as you approach your food?
I wish to hear the reason; please tell it to me. The bhikṣu replied: "Excellent, Son of the Buddha, you are able..."
Seeking the essentials of the Dharma, I shall now explain to you the method of eating. It has already been three days since I last ate.
Although I have obtained a small amount of food that may indeed be consumed, I observe that the faults and disadvantages of eating are exceedingly numerous; for this reason, I do not eat.
When a bhikṣu practices the Dharma, he does not cling to the myriad phenomena; he constantly takes compassion as his guiding scripture. By virtue of these causes and conditions, if one—
Whether in a monastic cell or beneath a tree, one must not consume any food at all without first cultivating a mind of profound equanimity and great compassion,
and universally bestowing it upon all. If one sees a guest monk arriving from afar who is utterly exhausted,

or others such as men and women, one should respectfully greet them, invite them to enter the dwelling, inquire after their well-being regarding cold, heat, hunger, and thirst, and provide prepared food according to one's ability.
One should provide material offerings so that they may eat. If there is no food, one should run about to seek out and procure food and drink, with the resolve that it be offered as an act of worship.
One should give food even by selling the three robes, selling a single alms bowl, or even selling one's own body.

This applies to all, including the solitary, the sick, the poor, the destitute, and beggars—both men and women—and extends even to cattle, horses, dogs, birds, and other animals; one should give universally so that all may be satisfied.
They give food to all, including insects and other creatures; yet they themselves do not constantly eat the hundred flavors, instead making others eat coarse and foul food.

Why is this? Because they harbor greed for food, providing it only for their own bodies and not sharing it with their retinue, nor bestowing it upon the wretched and hidden within their own persons, whereby the Buddha-nature and compassion are not allowed to manifest. When their physical lives end, they fall to the great earth.
In hell, or as a hungry ghost (*preta*), one undergoes various agonies for immeasurable eons. Fearing such retribution, one does not crave food.
There are two kinds of food: first, worldly food; second, supramundane food. One develops a profound sense of weary detachment toward worldly food.
The Buddha said: "Monks, when one desires to eat, it is truly terrifying. Food is the source of suffering; food is the root of anxiety.
That birth and death increase is brought about by food. This dependent body, composed of the four great elements, exists because of afflictions and because of evil karma.
Relying on food, life is sustained; relying on life, craving arises. Though one receives food and drink merely to provide for this precarious life,"
Furthermore, one must not give rise to even a single thought of attachment. The Buddha permitted bhikṣus to eat in a single sitting;

as for this practice of eating in a single sitting, my cultivation of fields, storage of wealth, and so forth cannot suffice for food. One should simply maintain a single alms bowl and beg for food when it is time to eat.
If there is a person who gives, one may eat their food. If a person does not give, one should consider my own karmic retribution. Why is this?

Even when the Śākya Tathāgata, the unsurpassed field of merit, went begging and returned with an empty bowl, how much more so for other ordinary beings of meager merit who are certain to receive food?
Reflecting thus, one should not beg again. When food is obtained...
It may be divided into four parts. First, take one part to offer with reverent faith to the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the worthy sages of the Three Vehicles throughout the ten directions.
Make this great vow: "From beginningless time until this day, I have held the false view of denying cause and effect and have committed unwholesome acts.
I failed to practice giving and failed to make offerings to the Buddhas. By these causes and conditions, I have been poor in birth after birth."
I am impoverished and lowly, lacking any power or influence; I have not encountered the Buddhas nor heard the Dharma, and I constantly dwell in the evil realms as if wandering through a garden.
Now, I offer this food to the Triple Gem; may you receive it out of compassion through the power of your great mercy.
May I and all sentient beings be freed from the cycle of birth and death. Next, I offer one portion to my parents, teachers, elders, and friends for seven generations.
Regarding these four debts of gratitude: next, with one portion, he universally bestows [offerings] upon all sentient beings of the six realms and all conscious creatures of the four modes of birth.
Moved by boundless, supreme great compassion, he universally covers all of them and makes this vow: "The retributions of sentient beings in the six realms are most wretched.
Sentient beings in the hells eat balls of extreme heat, which constantly damage their bodies. As for what they eat..."
How can one take pleasure in attachment to birth? The class of hungry ghosts (preta) is constantly exhausted by hunger, receiving only filth such as excrement and urine;
for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas they do not obtain these things again. Even if they should obtain a small portion, it is immediately lost;

how much less could they obtain subtle, wondrous, and pure food and drink? As for animals and asuras, they have food according to their respective lot, yet because they harbor mutual ill will, they cannot obtain it.
May they eat in peace. The two classes of beings, humans and devas, have various kinds of food according to their respective karmic retributions;
because they give rise to craving and attachment, they in turn produce a mass of suffering. Thus, all such foods are accompanied by fear and are not to be relished.
Out of great compassion, I entreat all the Buddhas to sprinkle the water of wisdom upon the food to purify it, and bestow it upon all sentient beings.
Likewise, by bestowing the food of fearlessness, each attains peace and happiness.

Through these causes and conditions, may you and all others, in every successive birth, be born where you behold the Buddhas and hear the Dharma, always obtaining the joy of the Dharma and the food of dhyāna-pleasure, up until the ultimate fruit and virtue of nirvāṇa.
Reflecting thus, one universally bestows [this food] upon all. When about to eat one’s own portion, one immediately reflects: "Would it not be better to eat..."
One should conceive the thought that sand and gravel are sweet and delicious; one must not give rise to craving for this food.
It would be better to eat the marrow, bones, flesh, and liver of my own body while conceiving thoughts of peace and happiness than to harbor an attachment to this food.
What wise person would crave such sweet flavors, let alone seek them within my body? My precepts are incomplete, my diligence is not deep, and my patience is not thick; as for meditation...

One’s meditative concentration is not firm, one’s wisdom is not clear, and one’s compassion is not all-pervading. How can such a body, burdened by evil karma, receive the food offered by the faith of a donor?

Even if one were to pass through incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), eating glowing iron balls three times every day that burn the body and consume the bones and flesh, one would still be unable to eat the food of a donor with a mouth defiled by the breaking of precepts.
To consume such food is like taking a great poisonous drug, for it severs the life-force of wisdom; it is like wielding a sharp sword, for it cuts through the Dharma-body.
A bhikṣu should regard such food as he would an enemy brandishing a drawn sword, watching for an opportunity to strike; he should also view it with dread, as a deer does when seeing a hunter.
Exert effort, exert effort! One must not give rise to a mind of attachment. This world and the world beyond are utterly terrifying.
Reflecting thus, "I should not be attached to such faults," yet one still gives rise to a mind of attachment toward food.
Simply place it in my mouth and bite it with my teeth; having disciplined and focused the mind, then eat it. Furthermore, you should reflect:
"I am an ordinary person whose afflictions are deep and heavy, and thus I should not receive this food.

It is only because there are the Buddhas of the three bodies within my own body that they can accept and enjoy this offering. May the Buddhas within my body accept this food and drink, and cause the donor to [attain merit]."
May my primary vows be decisively fulfilled. Furthermore, I make this vow:

in order to sever all afflictive and cognitive obscurations—both the delusions of conceptualizing phenomena and their underlying reality, and both the innate and the intellectually acquired—I now eat this.
In order to extinguish all karma that is certain to be experienced as well as all indeterminate karma and so forth, I now eat this. In order to transform the entire mass of suffering, I now eat this.
Because the retribution of fragmented existence resulting from causes and conditions is utterly unbearable, I now eat this.

It is for the sake of realizing the fruit of Buddhahood—the Dharma-body, the Reward-body, and the Response-body—and for the purpose of delivering sentient beings so that they may enter the Buddha-way; it is for these reasons that I now eat it.
Having reflected thus, one then eats it; this is called mundane food. Furthermore, one also eats supramundane food, which is capable of being consumed.
That which is eaten is like an illusion or a dream; when its intrinsic nature is sought, it is entirely unapprehendable.
If one says that the mind of the past limit experiences this food, since that past-limit mind has already ceased, it is likewise unapprehendable.

If one says that the mind of the middle limit experiences this food, because the mind of the middle limit does not abide, it is likewise unapprehendable. If one says that the mind of the future limit experiences this... [it is likewise unapprehendable].
As for eating: because the mind of the future limit has not yet arisen, it likewise cannot be found within the internal or external mind, nor can it be found in objects.
Seeking the conditions for eating, they are all unfindable; it is like seeking the essential nature of space within space—it will ultimately remain unfindable throughout immeasurable eons.
Furthermore, observing that all phenomena are empty and quiescent is called "eating emptiness. It is like a person eating.

When the stomach is empty and spacious, one contemplates that although all phenomena (*dharma*) are empty, they nevertheless exist; that the myriad phenomena of the universe abide without being separate from one another—this is called "having food.
It is like when a person eats much and their belly is full. One then contemplates that all phenomena both exist and do not exist, and are neither existent nor non-existent.
They transcend the characteristics of words and are beyond the realm of conceptual thought. To contemplate phenomena in this way is called the Middle Way.

Regarding food: just as when a person eats, they take neither too little nor too much, but observe moderation so that the stomach remains at ease and one is free from the suffering of overeating or hunger.
If one were to discuss the relative superiority or inferiority among the three types of Dharma-food, contemplating food through the Middle Way is considered the foremost.
To contemplate the mind in this way, fully endowed with the Three Truths, is called the characteristic of Dharma-food; it is praised by all Buddhas of the three periods of time. All...
This is what Bodhisattvas consume. The noble ones of the Two Vehicles merely obtain empty food; they do not further obtain the latter two types of Dharma-food.
How much less could worldly humans, devas, or asuras even hear its name, let alone consume it?

If one does not contemplate in this way, it is not called "begging for food," nor is one counted among the ranks of the Saṃgha. One will not know the time of liberation in future lives; one can only...
This increases the cycle of birth and death in its fragmented form, just as pigs and sheep delight in their pens and latrines, further increasing their own stench and filth—this is truly pitiable.
You should receive this instruction: when you wish to eat, contemplate your mind in this way before eating.
Thus, you shall consume the food of afflictions, evil karma, and ignorance within the mind; the Dharma-food, the Dharma-body, and the life-force of wisdom will remain eternally present, never dying.
This Dharma-food causes his compassionate physical strength to increase even further. He extensively delivers sentient beings, causing them to realize the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Having finished speaking, the bhikṣu remained unmoving in body and mind, as if having entered meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), sitting serenely and upright.
Hearing what he had said, I prostrated with my head at his feet and praised him with various words of respect. The bhikṣu remained silent and spoke no further. After [a period of] time...
After seven days, as soon as he opened his eyes, he said, "Excellent, bhikṣu! You are still here. I shall demonstrate my supernatural powers to you, O śramaṇa.
He took the bowl and threw it out; at that moment, the bowl flew up into the air, emitting five-colored rays of light that circled and whirled about before descending back down.
When I saw that the bowl was filled with delicious food, the bhikṣu said to me: "I..."
I pay my deepest prostrations and give rise to profound faith in the power of such a path of begging for food.
For this reason, I now address my disciples: regarding the food of a single lifetime, the wise feel fear. You may eat twice or thrice daily;
otherwise, who will rescue you from the retribution of your sins in future lives? Alas, alas! Through food, the precept-breaking bhikṣu increases his karma and falls [into the lower realms].

Having undergone various extreme sufferings in the hells for immeasurable kalpas—just like a monkey that dies suddenly from eating the five bonds, or like a summer insect that sees light, feels desire, enters the fire, and perishes—you were greatly deluded and most pitiable.
Now, arouse a heart of great shame and remorse; abandon the thought of eating much, and practice with courageous diligence.
He restrained the three types of action. Upon hearing the Great Master’s teaching, the disciple bhikṣu made a vow before the Buddha:
"From this day forth until the signs of death appear, I shall eat but one meal per sitting and restrain my mind with diligence, just like that bhikṣu who went for alms in the past."

Therefore, one does not regress from cultivation thereafter and attains the purification of the six sense faculties. If there is a bhikṣu seeking the Buddha-way, he should practice such contemplation before partaking of food.
For this reason, one should know that the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings are non-differentiated in these three respects.
One should contemplate the true thusness of the dharma-nature as quiescent, for all phenomena arise from the mind in an inconceivable manner.
The Venerable Myōchi asked a bhikṣu, "What is the essential principle of the dharmas practiced by a śramaṇa?
The bhikṣu replied, "I constantly read and recite the sūtras every day; they number several hundred fascicles, and I never retreat from them. The Venerable Myōchi then asked:
With what state of mind does one recite and chant the sūtras? A bhikṣu said, "By nature I am clever; I naturally memorize and recite the sūtras when I read them.
Seeing that all Dharma masters read and chant the sūtras, I now read and chant because they are Dharma masters.
He did not understand the subtle causes and conditions for his recitation. The wise Preceptor said to the bhikṣu, "It is rare and difficult to encounter [such a person]."

"Riding upon the sūtras—your current recitation is indeed a difficult task. However, you do not know the mental conduct or the ritual methods for recitation, which is why I have been sighing and reflecting.
I shall now show you the method of recitation. I am the son of a high minister from a Hu kingdom;

having grown weary of the world, I left the household life to renounce pleasure and seek the Dharma. Although I recited the sūtras when I first resolved my mind [to attain enlightenment], I did not yet know how to contemplate them."
Dharma: To the north of the Hu kingdom, there was a bhikṣu on a mountain. I went to that mountain to practice walking meditation and recite the scriptures.
At that time, the bhikṣu had bathed his body and mind and put on fresh, clean robes, having cast off his soiled garments.
Before the scripture scrolls, he burned incense, scattered flowers, and prostrated to the scriptures hundreds of thousands of times. Thereafter, he sat upright and composedly upon the Dharma seat.
He applied famous incense to his hands and respectfully took up the sūtra; he held it aloft above his head, reciting and contemplating it without raising his voice.
Furthermore, he did not read early in the day; throughout the entire day, he would finish only one fascicle, or perhaps half a fascicle.

Having finished reading, he would set the sūtra down and close his eyes to contemplate. Rising from the Dharma-seat, he prostrated before the sūtra as before hundreds of thousands of times, weeping with grief.
Longing with thirst, he returned to his dwelling, removed his *pāṭha-vastra* (reading robe), and donned his ordinary garments. In this manner, day after day, he did not desist.
Seeing him thus engaged in the practice of recitation, I wished to know the underlying cause and asked that bhikṣu.
The bhikṣu replied, "You are a newly ordained monk; therefore, you do not know the cause. I shall explain it for you. Generally, regarding the recitation..."
There are two methods of recitation: first, recitation by means of written characters; second, recitation through contemplation of the principle. Regarding recitation by means of written characters:
if one wishes to recite a sutra, one should purify the two karmas [of body and speech]. Why is this? Because to take up a sutra with defiled hands or to face a sutra with a foul mouth [is improper].
In future lives, one may be born as a dung-worm in a latrine, or fall into hell where hands and mouth are broken and one must drink molten copper.
Therefore, you must certainly purify your body, hands, and mouth; you should know this deeply. This sutra is the parent of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
That which is the teacher of all Buddhas is the so-called Mahāyāna.
One should know that the Dharmakāya Tathāgata is present wherever the entire body-relics, the sūtra scrolls, and the assemblies of Buddhas abide, surrounded by nāgas and devas.
Therefore, the reader must apply their mind with full dignity and purity of hand and mouth; they should smear their hands with fragrant incense and hold aloeswood and sandalwood in their mouth.

Let all [negative] breaths be extinguished. Conceive the thought that [this opportunity] is difficult to encounter. Mentally reflect and verbally recite: "I now contemplate the faults of birth and death.
For kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, I have fallen into the three evil realms; from darkness into further darkness, I have increased my various karmic afflictions.
Thus, I have not even heard the names of heaven, earth, sun, moon, or parents, nor have I heard the teachings of the five precepts and ten wholesome deeds for humans and devas."
How much more so, then, to hear such a Dharma-gate of the true reality of the Mahāyāna! Difficult is the appearance of a Buddha in the world;

difficult is it for the Buddha to preach this; difficult is it even to hear its name; great is the difficulty for one to read and uphold it; rare is the awakening to the World-Honored One’s marvelous appearance in the world;
and rare is the contemplation of the skillful means by which he established the Mahāyāna. That we have encountered such a Dharma is like [the emergence of] the blind turtle—
It was as if encountering a hollow in a floating log, like a poor person obtaining a wish-fulfilling jewel; thus, with such longing and devotion, no other thoughts arose.
Furthermore, he repented of the transgressions committed through the three karmas and made a great vow, endowed with a heart of compassion.

According to his capacity, he offered incense, flowers, food, drink, banners, canopies, and ritual implements to the sutra scrolls. When it came time to read and recite them, he prostrated himself on the ground with his five limbs touching the earth.
Having paid homage to the scripture scrolls, one should sit upon the Dharma seat and contemplate at the appropriate time.

Although it is the body of an ordinary person, because one now reads the Mahāyāna and desires to hear the sutra, the eight classes of beings, including nāgas and devas, all assemble; the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas fill the void to bear witness.
Therefore, with a heart of pure faith, I should now recite the sutras.
While contemplating in this manner during the recitation, one can trace the phrases and sentences without further confusion, nor omit a single word or character.
Faith arises equally throughout the beginning, middle, and end, and does not regress. Such recitation is called "recitation as an activity" and "recitation through contemplation of the mind."

The meaning of this is exceedingly profound. By shattering the subtle dust of the mind, one brings forth the Great Thousand-fold Sūtra. Thus, one knows that the sūtra scrolls exist only within my own heart;
my physical body is itself the sūtra scroll: the marrow is like the axle, the skin and flesh are like the paper, and the color of blood is like the ink.

The five viscera and six bowels, such as the liver and so forth, exist in infinite distinctions, layered upon one another without confusion, just as the characters in a scripture are infinite in number yet do not intermingle or become disordered.
The sovereign mind dwells within them, its nature profound and mysterious; is this not the true reality (*tathatā*) expounded in the scriptures?
The Buddha’s teaching on the inconceivable principle of the good and evil of the sentient beings' mind-nature is called [the *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra*].
Sūtra scroll. Therefore, one should know this: who can speak of a sūtra scroll? Who can speak of sentient beings? Their names differ, but their essence is the same;
they are like the difference between "eye" and "organ of sight. Thus, my own body is the sūtra scroll, and my own mind is the true reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa) that it explicates.
To perceive and know in this way is the true sūtra scroll; to contemplate in this way is the true recitation. This is for the purpose of causing sentient beings to know their own minds.
As for "sūtra scrolls," they are called sūtra scrolls because they are taught through skillful means (*upāya*).

Furthermore, one must contemplate that both my body, which performs the recitation, and the sūtra scrolls being recited are like magical illusions (*māyā*) and cannot be found in reality. Who is it that reads and recites? Who is it that listens to the sūtra?

It is like the sounds produced by a magically created person within a dream, or like an echo arising from a sound in a mountain valley. Therefore, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena (*dharmas*) is empty.
Reciting and chanting in this manner is called "reciting the contemplation of emptiness. Although it is empty, it exists:

my body, the scripture, the sounds of recitation and chanting, and the hearing of these sounds—both great and small—do not perish due to karma, but abide spontaneously. Therefore, although all phenomena are empty, they exist.
The sounds of my body’s recitation and chanting of the sutra scrolls are heard; whether great or small, they do not lose their causal efficacy through karma, but abide spontaneously.
Therefore, although the myriad teachings are empty, they nonetheless exist. To contemplate in this manner is called "contemplative recitation of the sutra scrolls.
My body and all phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent, neither both existent and non-existent, and are not objects known by consciousness, nor can they be fully expressed by words.

The dharmas are quiescent from beginningless time, as they naturally are. Therefore, within the very mind that reads the sūtras for even a moment, the realm of sentient beings and the fruit of Buddhahood are spontaneously complete;
the six perfections and the myriad practices exist as they naturally are. Thus one recites the Mahāyāna sūtras.
To read the scriptures while contemplating the Middle Way within the mind, and to abide in such contemplation, is called "reading and reciting according to principle.

Even merely reciting the words of the scriptures while regulating the three karmas yields boundless merit; how much more so for reading and reciting in correspondence with the contemplation of the mind!
The extent of the merit thus obtained is beyond measure; only a Tathāgata knows its magnitude, for it is beyond the reach of calculation by ordinary intellects.
All those who read in this manner should offer them worship, prostrations, and praise. You must listen deeply to these two methods of reciting the scriptures;
take them into your heart and store them there, lest they be lost. When the bhikṣu had finished speaking, he entered the night to recite the sūtras.
From his mouth issued a five-colored radiance that filled and illuminated the interior of the room. I beheld this sign even more clearly.
Faith and reverence arose, and no further doubt remained. From that time forward, whenever he read the sutras, he recited them according to those methods.
Monks should likewise recite the Mahāyāna according to these methods; by doing so, they will achieve the Buddha-body endowed with myriad virtues in their present existence.
Even if one recites the Mahāyāna for many kalpas, if one does not rely on the contemplation of the mind and does not recite according to the Dharma, I fear it will only become a remote cause.

It brings no great benefit. It is like a person who has fallen ill and obtained an excellent, superior medicine, yet does not know how to compound it, nor understands the method for preparing eye-salve.
Merely rejoicing at having acquired this subtle and excellent medicine, they take it as they please;

unaware of the proper time for treatment, the medicine turns into poison and their illness and suffering increase further. They may suffer death-like agony or even die. Although they have barely survived, the excellent medicine...

The medicine has exhausted its power. Therefore, the bhikṣu was able to understand the method: to take the medicine of the Mahāyāna to treat the disease of afflictions, thereby increasing the life-force of the three bodies.
Upon hearing this, the bhikṣu prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground; he fainted and his breath ceased.
Water was sprinkled upon his face, and he returned to life. "Alas! How tragic! This body of evil karma did not know such a profound Dharma until now. I—
Now, for the first time, the flavor of the Dharma has been tasted and partaken. From this day forward, you shall uphold it thus. Furthermore, the Upādhyāya further admonishes the śramaṇas:
"This is a secret matter; do not transmit it to those who are not suitable vessels. The sentient beings of the final age have meager roots of goodness;

if they were to contemplate the mind in this way, they would not believe or accept it, but would instead give rise to slander. It is like sprinkling a single drop of water upon sands extending for ten thousand li."
It must not be moistened; how much more so for the sentient beings of the five turbidities in the final age who act in such and such ways.

Therefore, bhikṣus, listen with single-minded attention. Be sober and do not transmit it arbitrarily or without revealing its significance. Thus you should know that the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings are non-differentiated in these three respects.
You should contemplate the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the dharma-nature as quiescent, for all phenomena arise from the mind in an inconceivable manner.

The Yakṣa deity manifested to the bhikṣu and spoke. In the monastery of the Hu kingdom, there was a bhikṣu who dwelt beneath a tree.
For three days he wept in sorrow and distress, refusing to eat, and uttered words of cursing. The Yakṣa Dharmagupta appeared with half his body and addressed the bhikṣu, saying:
"For what reason do you weep in sorrow and abstain from food for several days? The bhikṣu replied: "I..."
"The three robes (*tricīvara*) are the most subtle and supreme. Among all three robes, these are the most excellent and wondrous.
For many years, I have guarded them firmly without losing them. Yet, having placed them in my room and gone out, they were stolen by another;
because I lost these wondrous possessions, I weep and lament, even to the point of fasting, and I curse that person. The yakṣa deity said, "O Bhikṣu, you are not right."
"O śramaṇa, you possess not the mind of a śramaṇa; you are not a disciple of the Śākya; you do not practice true brahmacarya. Why is this?
When one seeks the dharma of a bhikṣu, even at the cost of losing one's life, one should not give rise to longing;
how much less so for other things such as dwellings, bedding, food and drink, medicine, the three robes, and the alms bowl? For what reason do you cling to such trifling objects? Thus he spoke.
When you later suffer the consequences of your various evil karmas, who will rescue you? O Bhikṣus, do not utter curses;

instead, keep the Buddhas in mind and seek the wealth of the Dharma. You should know that in the kingdom of Saṃghāṭa there is a śramaṇa named Nakula, who is fully endowed with ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
His compassion and dhyāna-concentration are perfected and matured, and his fame is renowned within [the realm].
He was highly respected by the assembly outside [the monastery].

At that time, a king came to the bhikṣu’s dwelling and respectfully made offerings of various precious objects, namely gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and so forth, as well as garments, white woolen cloth, and many other treasures.
After making such offerings, when the king was returning to his palace, Nāgadatta desired to give those various treasures and wealth to one person.
All were impoverished and solitary. As the sun set and night fell during the hour of Hai (10 p.m.), more than several dozen bandits suddenly entered in a chaotic manner to seize various goods.
They further plundered the monastic robes—the three robes and the alms bowl—and having taken whatever they desired from the room, departed.
At that time, Nakula saw that there was not a single thing remaining within the room, and he beheld my person.
They were naked and without clothing; nevertheless, no sorrow arose in their hearts, their complexions were radiant, and their chests were filled with joy.
Seeing a house, they took a piece of fallen lapis lazuli. When the bhikṣu saw this, he was struck with fear and seized the gem, running out and crying out, "Thieves!
Wait, wait! You all! Hearing the bhikṣu’s cry, the thieves stood still for a moment. The bhikṣu...
With joy, he gave the jade to the thieves, saying, "Why do you not take this jade? Among the seven treasures, its radiance is most excellent.
At that time, the thieves marveled at the monk’s conduct and asked him, "Do you feel no stinginess or attachment toward this wealth?
The monk replied, "I now harbor no desire for these jewels; I regard them as mere riches."
"Just like a heap of filth, how could one who conceives a thought of revulsion and renunciation give rise to craving? Excellent! You have swept away my impurities.

When the wicked bandits heard the bhikṣu’s words, they all felt shame and remorse, and each consulted with the others, saying, "Who would feel such weary detachment toward such a multitude of treasures?
Let us cease our greed and refrain from committing evil deeds; instead, we shall return these various precious objects to the bhikṣu."

The bhikṣus did not accept it. They enticed the thieves to take it, but the people would not take the offerings and instead returned them to the bhikṣus. Thus, as time passed, they continued to refuse each other's wealth.
The bandits addressed the Saṃgha, saying: "Among the beings of this world—whether kings, ministers, śramaṇas, or householders—"
"All people delight in wealth and treasures; they seek them with all their might until, approaching old age, they sigh in regret.
For what reason, O bhikṣu, do you not seek wealth, but instead give rise to revulsion toward it as if seeing a poisonous drug? The bhikṣu replied, "Can you hear this?"
I shall now explain this for you. All sentient beings in the world are deluded regarding birth and death;

they grasp at impermanent bodies as being permanent and seek ephemeral wealth like floating clouds, which only serves to increase their suffering and transgressions. Those whom one beheld yesterday are gone today; the person seen in the morning is no longer seen by night.
Whether king or minister, who can escape this calamity? Entering the sea or ascending to the heavens, one cannot avoid death.
With such a body, one greedily accumulates wealth and stores it away; yet a small spark of fire may consume it in an instant, or the waters of the sea may carry it away, vanishing in a moment.
In seeking material goods, one instead gives rise to sorrow and affliction, bowing one's head in sighs and shedding tears out of stinginess.
The fire of desire burns the chest, and the waters of desire drown the body. When will these scattered riches ever be returned? In this present life, they are utterly destroyed.

The liver produces evil karma. Due to the causal conditions of the evil karma of craving wealth and treasures, at the end of life one enters the Avīci and other hells to undergo various extreme sufferings.
Fierce fires burn the body, with flames erupting from every joint. One may ascend the Sword Tree or scale the Mountain of Blades;
one may be cast into boiling cauldrons or enter the River of Ashes; one may eat boiling excrement or devour iron balls; or one may drink...

Molten copper may be poured over them, or they may be made to lie upon iron beds; some are forced to embrace copper pillars or copper forests until their bodies are shattered, while glowing hot pellets burn out their eyes.

Such sufferings as these are all gathered upon a single body. Raising their voices in wailing, they cry out, "Who will bestow a heart of compassion? Their livers are crushed with grief and lamentation, yet they cannot escape.
Hardly have they left hell when they are reborn among the hungry ghosts (preta). Due to the karmic conditions of their greed for wealth and treasures, their vital essence is utterly exhausted.
Starving and parched, they seek food throughout the ten directions but find nothing more than fire and charcoal to eat, which burns their bodies as they weep in sorrow.
Or they drink dew that suddenly turns into pus and blood; or their entire bodies are melted by molten copper and set ablaze; or as they run about, fire flows from beneath their feet.
Such sufferings are beyond counting. For the sake of fleeting, floating wealth, humans endure these for a brief moment, only to fall into the three miserable realms.
Thus one suffers for many eons. Therefore, the wise see wealth and renounce it with detachment; the foolish, however, love wealth and give rise to attachment.
The Great Teacher Śākyamuni instructed the bhikṣus, saying: "O bhikṣus, do not seek sensual pleasures. You should give rise to wearying detachment toward all phenomena.
Contemplate the body as being like foam; contemplate life as being like dew; contemplate wealth and possessions as being like a magical illusion."
Cloud-like Reflections: Contemplate men and women as being born in hell; contemplate food as worms; contemplate soup as excrement;
contemplate the monastic quarters as being like emerging from prison; contemplate one's kin as being led away to hell;
contemplate clothing as snake skins; and contemplate alms bowls as skulls. To the point that even in dreams, no craving or pleasure arises. Why is this so?
Because there is much suffering, a bhikṣu always makes few desires and contentment his practice. Therefore, I now do not covet wealth or treasures;
I do not give rise to even a single thought of attachment toward my own body or life, let alone toward other transient riches that are like floating clouds.
When the bandits heard the bhikṣu’s words, their minds were opened and they wept; they reproached themselves and repented.
Having passed [that time], they sought ordination. The bhikṣus rejoiced and shaved their heads, conferring the precepts upon them.
Once the bandits had become ordained, they said to the śramaṇas: "We have left the household life to become disciples of the Buddha.

As the Great Master has taught, there is no pleasure to be found in any thing whatsoever. If that is so, then as śramaṇas we should have nothing to enjoy. The bhikṣus replied: "Excellent, you [have spoken well]."
They are able to inquire about the practices and procedures of the bhikṣus. However, the disciples of the Buddha do not give rise to attachment toward any phenomena;

they do not even give rise to attachment toward the Buddha-dharma, let alone toward other dharmas. Yet, for the sake of benefiting others through great compassion, they seek the Buddha-dharma with various skillful means.
If one gives rise to practices for self-benefit, it becomes an obstacle to great compassion; therefore, one must resolutely seek the Buddha-dharma.
The Dharma is solely for the sake of sentient beings; one should contemplate it thus with compassion. When facing food, seek only the joy of the Dharma and the bliss of dhyāna;
when seeing clothing, seek only the robe of patience; dwell without attachment, seeking only to abide in the chamber of compassion.
Seeing one's kinsmen, one does not give rise to attachment or craving; one aspires for the attendants of the myriad practices as skillful means.

Regarding the body, one seeks only the Dharma-body of the myriad virtues; regarding this dew-like life, one seeks only the life of wisdom. Although one seeks the Buddha-dharma, one does not give rise to attachment to the Dharma.

How much more so regarding other dharmas—how could one give rise to even a single thought of attachment? Listen well, bhikṣu: the sufferings of household life are manifold and cannot be fully enumerated.
There is the suffering of the hardships of royal law; the suffering of being entangled by wife and children; the suffering of being oppressed by kinsmen; the suffering of lacking official rank;

the suffering of not being satiated with wealth; the suffering of seeking all manner of things; the suffering of separation from the beloved; the suffering of encountering the hateful; and the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks. Such are these various [sufferings].
Suffering increases day by day and presses in night after night; though it is suffering, they seek it and do not give rise to weary detachment, vying with one another to pursue it.
It is like a thirsty person drinking salt water: their thirst only increases further, and they seek more salt water.

It is also like a great garden latrine that is exceedingly pleasant to those who have left the household life; they seek to escape the suffering of kingly calamities and thereby bring about the state of the Dharma King.
In this state, one is free from the suffering of wife and children and attains true brahmacarya. Having few desires and being content, one is free from the suffering of hunger and lack.

Having left the home of affection and love, one is free from the suffering of separation. Deeply generating compassion, one is free from the suffering of enmity and hatred. Above, one receives the Tathāgata’s protection through the touch of his hand upon the crown of the head;
in the middle, one dwells in constant peace and joy together with all bodhisattvas; and below, one is revered by devas, humans, nāgas, yakṣas, and others.
Reverence and respect [for them]. Such joys as these cannot be fully described. Excellent!

May you all enter such a realm of peace and bliss, practice according to the Dharma, and realize great awakening. As for those bandit-like bhikṣus who accept and practice [the teachings], they shall all see that the Path is far away.
Before that community of bhikṣus has entered parinirvāṇa, we shall constantly protect them and never depart from their side.
"I see now that you are practitioners of great evil, like thieves among bhikṣus who have long harbored shamelessness.

You should not give rise to suffering over the loss of the three robes; instead, you should deeply contemplate the Dharma-robe of the Mahāyāna mind, rather than giving rise to attachment for the conditioned robes of the three garments.
Having spoken these words, the yakṣa vanished. Upon hearing this, the bhikṣu felt profound remorse and gave rise to the unsurpassed resolve.
One’s resolve seeks the Buddha-dharma; therefore, one should know that mind, Buddha, and sentient beings are non-differentiated in these three respects.
One should contemplate the quiescence of the *dharmatā* and *tathatā*, for all phenomena arise from the mind in an inconceivable manner.
The Admonition of Dharma Master Fachong to His Disciples: Dharma Master Fachong had a disciple who did not study the orthodox teachings nor recite the sūtras;
the only dhāraṇī he was fond of reciting was one particular one. The Master spoke privately to that disciple, saying:
"Regarding this *Acalanātha-mantra* which you recite and maintain, apart from this, what other intention or practice do you have for your recitation?"
"This is the mantra. Furthermore, how many mantras do you recite each day? The disciple replied: "By the power of this incantation, I have received the protection of the Vidyārāja.
Birds suddenly fell from flight, and flowing rivers were brought to a standstill. Dragons and spirits were bound, and the King was compelled to look up [in submission].
With such a mind, I maintain and recite this mantra, chanting it one thousand times each day and night. Thus admonished by Dharma-chong Heshang.
The disciple said: "Do not harbor such hopes anymore. This body is like a flash of lightning, remaining for only a brief moment;

life is like dew upon the grass, vanishing by morning after being placed there at night. One's majestic power, strength, wealth, and prime of youth—all do not follow the body, nor do they abide permanently.
Why do you not contemplate impermanence with this body? A human birth is difficult to obtain, and the Buddha-dharma is difficult to encounter."

"Because you recite a single dhāraṇī merely for the sake of empty worldly hopes while disregarding future lives—if you were instead to overturn these worldly expectations, resolve to seek the Buddha-way, and fear the three miserable realms, I shall now explain the method for upholding the mantra.
The disciple replied, "I am currently ignorant and know nothing at all; only upon hearing the Great Master’s admonition do I first realize impermanence. Excellent!"
"O Upādhyāya, please explain this to me. I seek only the path of the Buddha and do not delight in worldly pleasures. The Upādhyāya replied, "So it is, so it is.
What virtuous person would not follow wholesome words? In the past, when I encountered a wise man, I followed him and stayed with him for one night.
That bhikṣu did not sleep throughout the entire night, but sat upright, constantly shedding tears as he wept."
I frequently heard his voice; he was constantly snapping his fingers, sighing in lamentation, and his complexion had turned pale. "My mind is not stained by the Dharma of Bodhi;

I merely and constantly hope for fame and profit. I recite a single mantra as my practice, while I recall that the people of the Buddha's lineage have become negligent in body and mind, just like the ritual practices you are currently performing. At that time, I beheld the conduct of that bhikṣu.
A strange and wondrous thought arose in him, and he asked about its cause and conditions: "For what reason does this bhikṣu constantly weep?

He takes no pleasure in any monastics or laypeople, whether poor or wealthy, noble or lowly, nor in travel, play, freedom, or entertainment. I wish to hear his explanation. The bhikṣu replied: "This body is not a source of pleasure;
it is the root of all suffering. What joy could there be in it? My heart rejoices because for immeasurable kalpas I have fallen [into the cycle of birth and death]."

In the hells, their bodies and bones are crushed and their five viscera are incinerated. Seeing the hell-wardens with their own eyes, they give rise to a mind of terror; hearing their reproaches, they do not know how to respond.
Their tongues taste hot pellets, their bodies embrace red-hot copper, and their feet tread upon fire; the grief in their hearts is unbearable.
Having barely escaped the hells, they further pass through the realms of hungry ghosts and animals. To obtain a human body is as rare as the *udumbara* flower. Even when such a body is attained...
"This body is impoverished and lowly; being foolish and breaking the precepts, it returns to hell. It is like a person taking a stone and throwing it upward into the sky;
before long, it falls back to the ground. With such a body, how can one give rise to thoughts of peace?
For this reason, I now constantly harbor sorrow. Upon hearing these words, my body was struck with trembling, and I did not know where to turn. O Wise One!
"If one fears even the sufferings of the three miserable realms, how much more so for this ignorant body? Furthermore, what method is there to escape birth and death?
The bhikṣu replied: "You should recite mantras; this is the path to attaining Buddhahood. Merely aspire to the Pure Land of bliss, and I shall explain to you the mental practice of recitation.
Regarding recitation, there is recitation based on phenomenal characteristics (*sō-sō nenju*) and recitation based on the principle of reality (*ri-shō nenju*). If you understand..."

This means that one should reach a state of non-delusion regarding the path to Bodhi. One should perform the recitation of the ritual forms and maintain perfect deportment, purifying both the internal and external.

One should offer incense, medicinal herbs, and ritual implements according to one's capacity. One should deeply contemplate the infinite great vows of the Honored One (the deity), preceded by the great compassion of all Buddhas which is unconditioned.
With compassionate love for sentient beings like that of a mother for her only child, one should illuminate ignorance with the light of wisdom.
One whose body is shrouded in darkness covers that body of broken precepts with the garment of *śīla*.

Thus, through great compassion, one does not abandon sentient beings, just as a compassionate mother does not abandon her sick child; she embraces, covers, nourishes, and protects them with tears of sorrow.

I pray only that the Tathāgata may ever be present at this place, leading my body forth and bringing it beyond birth and death. When reciting the mantra, one should hold the prayer beads in the hand and maintain clear mindfulness.
The mantra pervades all without confusion. One should form this thought: "The mantra I uphold is the secret speech of the Buddhas of the three times and ten directions.
Within a single mantra, all virtues are subsumed; one should simply cultivate faith and not engage in discrimination.
For the disease of the afflictions, the mantra acts as medicine; for the ocean of birth and death, the mantra acts as a boat; it is the provision for awakening and the state of nirvāṇa."
Regarding the fruit of virtue: one subdues the enemy Pāpīyān with the sword of mantra, and removes the suffering of poverty with the wealth of mantra.
Contemplating thus, one performs pure recitation. One may perform contemplation by counting the number of mantras;

for every single bead passed, one severs an affliction and realizes *samādhi*. By passing the hundred and eight beads, one severs the hundred and eight afflictions that obstruct the body. [Recite] one...
By reciting the mantra universally, one realizes the single samādhi; by reciting it one hundred and eight times, one attains the one hundred and eight samādhis.

Contemplating in this manner, neither too slowly nor too hurriedly, one may recite the mantra with the aspiration: "By this merit, may I certainly realize bodhi, and may self and others—whether enemies or kin—enter the secret treasury.
This matter of recitation is a secret affair; although it should not be shown to others, stinginess regarding the Dharma is a fault.
Therefore, it is taught that one must know this: one must not treat it lightly. The *mālā* and the mantra are not something external;

rather, my own body and mind are called the *mālā*, and they are also called the mantra. One should contemplate the *mālā* directly through my own body; furthermore, there is no need to seek out a separate recitation. Why is this?
Because if one examines my body, such as the six parts beginning with the head, there are three hundred and sixty [joints].

Various bones, skin, flesh, blood, liver, the five viscera, and the six bowels—these various things exist through their combination, just as a rosary exists through the combination of its one hundred and eight beads, or as the jade of the Dharma exists through the combination of the jades of the ten disciples.
The constituent parts of sentient beings are impermanent; they are provisionally maintained for the duration of a single lifetime without being destroyed. This, then, is life.
The faculties persist through continuity, like a rosary of various gems joined together; though they may be scattered, they remain because their underlying connection is not lost.
Upon examining my own body, I see that from birth it has naturally passed into old age and gradually approached decay.

When the "wind-sword" severs the joints and the life-faculty departs, the various faculties disintegrate. Once the body has been dispersed, it is just like a rosary; the days and months have passed in great number.
As time passes through its cycles, the threads decay and the jade beads break; they scatter in every direction, and one knows not where they have gone.
Thus, one should know that apart from the body, no other rosary can be sought. To observe in this manner is called the "rosary of conceptualization.

The syllables of the mantra depend upon sound for their provisional establishment; they may exist or they may not. Only the contemplation of the rosary itself may be used as the object of observation.
Contemplation. Furthermore, the "straight mind" (*ṛju-citta*) is called recitation (*japa*) and so forth; it is not a separate entity.
When one investigates the nature of the mind, it is the basis of all phenomena (*dharma*), just as the *darma* gem is the primary stone among prayer beads. All gems take this as their principal;
likewise, all mental factors (*caitta-dharma*)—whether universal, object-specific, root afflictions, secondary afflictions, or non-associated formations—are layered and interwoven within it.
The mixture of good and evil is never lost; they abide in succession, just like the one hundred and eight beads of a rosary.
Although the ten types of disciple-beads differ in their substance and appearance, they do not depart from one another but abide as a single category.

Likewise, the various mind-kings (*citta-rāja*) and their mental factors (*caitta*), whether wholesome or unwholesome dharmas, are in their fundamental nature but a single *tathatā* (suchness), transcending the pursuit of goodness.
Evil arises from deluded conceptualization and the spontaneous activity of the discriminating mind, which is distinct from the primary mind (*citta*).

Furthermore, it is through the deluded mind that wholesome and unwholesome karma is produced, which draws forth the retributive fruits of good and evil within the three realms of existence. These manifest as a composite of birth and death throughout a single lifetime; they exist solely through the power of karma and deluded discrimination.
This is like the substance of the beads on a rosary: although there is no inherent essence of "large" or "small" in the jade itself, [the distinctions arise from the carving].
They are distinct. However, they abide in conjunction through the skillful application of craftsmanship and the binding of threads.

Therefore, when one contemplates this, the mind is like a large gemstone, the mental factors (*caitta*) are like the various smaller gems, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is like the craftsman, and the power of karma (*karmabala*) is like the threads.

The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) has no beginning, yet the wheel of delusion begins [to turn]. It is like a rosary encircling [the beads] to count them; it began with Dharma. Ignorance (*avidyā*) is without beginning and without end.
The discourse on the theory of severance concludes here. It is like a rosary that, having completed its circuit, ends differently;

it leaves behind the *dharma*. The nature of the mind is inconceivable; through cultivation, one becomes a Buddha. The ultimate, supreme stage is like holding a rosary upon the crown of the head; the nature of the mind is immeasurable.
As for the status of Bodhisattvas and noble sages, it is like a rosary tied around the neck;
at times their mental nature perceives the fruits of humans and devas, just as a rosary is worn upon the arm. At other times, their mental nature sinks into the three miserable realms.

It is like a rosary that has mistakenly fallen into the mud. At times, the nature of the mind is perfumed by the fragrance of the precepts, which is most delightful—just as a rosary enters sandalwood or aloeswood, its substance becomes exceedingly fragrant.

At other times, the nature of the mind is habituated by afflictions, which are most loathsome and to be shunned—just as a rosary comes into contact with onions, leeks, and the like, or falls into filth, its odor becomes exceedingly foul.
The nature of the mind is unstable; changing from moment to moment, it is difficult to discern. It may be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate;
it may ascend, descend, or remain in the middle; it may be distracted, concentrated, deluded, or wise. Although it is distinguished in these ways, [it remains the same].
Contemplating their fundamental nature, they are all one with the Dharma-realm and are truly difficult to conceive. They are like prayer beads, existing independently and without fixed form;
sometimes long or short, sometimes square or round; at times lost and scattered, and at other times recovered.
Although there are such various differences, if one traces them back to their origin, they emerge solely from the golden mouth of the Tathāgata’s teaching, and are not for ordinary people.

Recite thus. This method of contemplating the mantra-bead of the Heart Mantra is called "contemplative recitation" (*manasajapa*). The characteristics of the mantra syllables should be understood through prior visualization;
however, fearing that they may be kept secret, I shall not discuss the specific mantras here.
