Because of awakening, one gives rise to the distinctions between self and other; one generates thoughts of good and evil, harbors mutual resentment and enmity, and kills and harms one another from life to life, yet embraces joy in each other's presence and speaks of kinship wherever they go.
Contemplating such signs as being like illusions or the moon reflected in water, one reflects in this way:
although seeing an enemy, one does not give rise to an evil mind; although seeing one’s own body, one does not [give rise to attachment].
With loving-kindness, one views emptiness as empty, free from the notions of sorrow or joy, just as a conjured person sees another conjured person.
One merely takes pity on the delusions and confusions of one's own and others' false imaginings, never seeking out the faults or evils of sentient beings. Self and other are equal and inconceivable;

the three periods of time are not eternally separated within a single thought-moment. Thus, even when a wise person traverses the realms of the ten thousand dharmas, they immediately realize the reality.
By observing the mind in this manner, evil thoughts do not arise.

Compassion and patience increase and reach perfection moment by moment, instant by instant, like the lunar disc gradually becoming full, or like the sunlight shining everywhere throughout space without obstruction.
As I now directly observe the nature of the mind, even if I am subjected to your insults and blades—
"Carrying the staff, do not give rise to evil again; instead, cultivate compassion ever more deeply. You bhikṣus, if you possess a virtuous mind, quickly distance yourselves from an evil mind.

Practice and train in this way: this single life is like a dream. For what reason are you indolent and break the precepts? When the monks heard the bhikṣu speak thus, tears flowed from their eyes as blood.
They forever resolved upon the path of enlightenment, all upheld the prohibitive precepts, constantly cultivated patience, and gave rise to no further evil."
"O Bhikṣu, you should know that by reflecting in this way, one brings evil thoughts to eternal rest, just as the Saṃgha of old did.
After these words had been spoken, the yakṣa vanished. Having heard these words, from that time forth I constantly restrained my body and mind, fearing the future life.
Even when subjected to blows with sticks, abuse, or slander, I accepted them in silence without retaliating. At that time, the world...
People call me "One Who Embraces Patience. If there are bhikṣus who have resolved their minds on the Way, they should necessarily study and learn by contemplating the Dharma in this manner.
Therefore, one should know that the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings are non-differentiated in these three aspects.
One should contemplate the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) as quiescent, for all phenomena arise from the mind in an inconceivable manner.
The Venerable Fazhi asked a bhikṣu, "The practices of a Dharma Master are various and immeasurable. What kind of merit does a śramaṇa practice?
The bhikṣu replied, "I study the texts of the Dharma; preaching the Dharma and debating its meaning constitute my practice.
The Venerable asked, "If preaching the Dharma and debating its meaning lead to liberation from birth and death, this is a most excellent practice that one should surely follow."
"Joy. With what mental orientation should this practice be cultivated? The bhikṣu replied: "When during the exposition of the Dharma or the discussion of its meaning, one thinks within the mind:
'May all who hear the Dharma feel sympathetic joy; may they respect me and pay homage to me.'"
"Among the wise, I alone am supreme; my fame is renowned everywhere, and I receive all manner of offerings while attending to my followers throughout my life.
With such a mind, I preach the Dharma and engage in debate. Beyond this, what else could there be to enjoy?
The Upādhyāya replied, "When I hear you speak thus, it shatters my heart; it is unbearable. This is the practice of a śramaṇa."

One studies the Dharma-gates of the Tripiṭaka, yet why is it that the eye of wisdom becomes clouded by fame and profit? It is like having eyes but drinking wine until one is intoxicated and disordered;
or like being poisoned and losing one's mind, so that the eyes roll about without seeing forms.

Now we see that although these bhikṣus possess a modicum of wisdom, when they preach the Dharma and engage in debate, they drink the wine of fame and profit and consume the poison of seeking victory over others. Thus, intoxicated, disordered, and bewildered, they do not perceive the Two Truths.
The physical form resulting from the retribution of worldly sinful karma is likewise so. Among all sinful karmas, preaching the Dharma that is impure is the foremost and most gravely evil karma.
I shall now explain for you the profound methods for preaching the Dharma and engaging in doctrinal discussion.
Long ago, as I was traveling through various countries on foot, I went to a remote borderland where there was a bhikṣu named Śāntamati who upheld the Bodhi...
He strictly observed the bodhisattva precepts, guarding their essence with depth and never violating even the minor rules, let alone the ten grave ones.
He studied the Mahāyāna, possessing profound wisdom, gentle speech, and the most excellent eloquence. The monastic community of the kingdom all came to follow his teachings;

they abandoned their practice of facing south and instead performed prostrations toward him. I went to that place to attend upon him and stayed for a short time. At that time, the king and ministers of the country...
The assembly of laypeople, monks, and nuns all gathered together and addressed the bhikṣu, saying, "Excellent!
Today we would like you to preach the subtle and wondrous Dharma so as to gladden our hearts. The bhikṣu declined and did not preach the Dharma further.

In this manner, although the great multitude invited him every day with earnest persistence, the bhikṣu repeatedly declined their request and would not speak. At that time, the great assembly was filled with great distress.

He reflected, his tears falling as he wept in sorrow, finding no joy in his former abode. The śramaṇa Śāntamati, seeing these people seeking the Dharma with faith, gave rise to a heart of great compassion and accepted the assembly’s invitation.
Donning fresh, clean robes and becoming pure both inwardly and outwardly, he held an incense burner in his hand and proceeded slowly until he reached the hall door.
Closing his eyes in contemplation, he then entered the hall and performed the ritual prostrations according to the Dharma.
The Buddha ascended the high seat; with body upright, he entered into contemplation. He saw neither the great assembly nor the various forms before him, nor did he hear any other sounds.
As the time for preaching the Dharma approached, he raised his voice and wept bitterly, his tears flowing like a river.

When the gathered assembly of monastics and laypeople, noble and humble alike, saw the Silent Sage (Jñānaketu) weeping, they felt shame and remorse, though they did not understand the causes and conditions or the manner of his conduct. There was none who did not [feel this].
After those who were weeping had done so, he then expounded for them the profound and wondrous Dharma.

Without passing through long intervals, and in the space of but a single *muhūrta*, within that time all the great assembly conceived the thought of the Buddha toward Śāntamati and listened to the Dharma with a single mind.

Some wept with grief like calves who have lost their mothers; others rejoiced with joy like poor men who have found treasure; and others were struck with fear regarding the retribution for their sins.

Like a hunter who has caught a deer, some sought to leave the household life, some maintained the prohibitive precepts, some gathered their distracted minds, and some gave rise to the aspiration for the Way.
Others withdrew to live in seclusion, some practiced giving, and others repented of their manifold transgressions. Such instances of benefit were exceedingly numerous.
At that time, a wondrous fragrance filled the hall, and the sound of music was heard from afar in the air; before them, extraordinary sights appeared.
They conceived a sense of rare wonder. When the Bhikṣu Śāntamati had finished preaching the Dharma, he closed his eyes and entered contemplation.
Raising his voice, he wept loudly as previously described. Descending from the Dharma-seat, he prostrated himself before all the Buddhas.
With eyes of great compassion, he looked upon the great assembly and gradually departed from the hall. His contemplative reflections were beyond description. At that time, I witnessed this...

The Dharma taught by the Buddha was forever different from the manner in which other monks teach the Dharma. His heart gave rise to joy, and seeking a quiet moment, he went to the place where Śāntamati was and asked him:
"I have heard that the Buddha’s teaching on the Dharma for the purpose of transforming beings is the practice of a bodhisattva."
"Great Master, for what reason did you repeatedly decline our request to preach the Dharma? Furthermore, why did you weep and grieve at both the beginning and the end of your teaching?
I pray that you will explain this to me, for I wish to know the causes and conditions.

When I asked this question, there were several dozen learned bhikṣus with some degree of wisdom seated in the assembly who were engaged in discourse on the Dharma. The śramaṇa Śāntamati answered my question, saying:
"Excellent, Bhikṣu! I shall explain it to you. Listen attentively and reflect upon it.
This is the Dharma practiced by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas for teaching the Dharma to liberate others. It is beyond the reach of ordinary people of shallow understanding. Why is this?

If one explains the essential points of the Dharma without measuring the capacity of the listener, the hearer will lose the benefit, and both the speaker and the teaching will be in vain. Therefore, Pūrṇamanas, teach the Dharma."
Having received the admonition of Vimalakīrti, Śāriputra was rebuked by the non-Buddhists.

Even though the noble ones of the two vehicles have severed all afflictive obstructions of the three realms and realized the principle of the emptiness of persons, they still incur such faults regarding the preaching of the Dharma when their minds are not free from attachment.
How much more so for an ordinary person who has not severed their afflictions, yet attempts to teach others with only a fragmentary wisdom!
It would be better to gouge out the blue-lotus eyes of all the Buddhas of the three periods of time with a sharp sword than to preach the Dharma to others with an impure mind.
It would be better to kill the sentient beings of the six realms across immeasurable worlds simultaneously with a mass of blades than to do so.
Furthermore, one must not dwell with a mind attached to signs while preaching the Dharma for others. Even if one were to commit all manner of grave offenses at once—
such as the ten non-virtues and the five deeds of immediate retribution—

and were to undergo limitless suffering in the Avīci Hell for immeasurable eons solely because of this impure mind of signs, one should nevertheless ascend the high seat and preach the Dharma for others.

Dharma! It would be better for me to have my tongue pulled out with iron tongs, or for my tongue-root to be pierced and crushed with an extremely sharp sword until it is like fine dust, enduring such agony day and night, moment by moment, throughout immeasurable kalpas.
I should never again preach the Dharma or engage in debate with a mind that seeks fame and profit over the impure hearts of others. How tragic, how tragic! This is the age of turbidity.
I do not know the correct principles of the ultimate orthodox teaching, nor do I measure the differences in the faculties and capacities of sentient beings.
Driven solely by a poisonous mind that seeks fame and profit to surpass others, I manifest the appearance of teaching the Dharma to deceive and delude the world.

I plunder wealth and treasures for the sustenance of life and the adornment of my body, supporting my retinue and receiving the respect, prostrations, and offerings of others; yet, in truth, I possess neither wisdom nor virtuous conduct.
They are like bamboo and reeds that appear virtuous on the outside, yet are seen to be hollow within; they are also like painted jars filled with excrement and urine, unfit to be near one's person.
How truly lamentable it is! What kind of suffering will these teachers who preach the Dharma undergo in their future lives?

Who among the wise would delight in preaching the Dharma? Even if one does not give rise to a mind characterized by signs (*nimitta*), as long as delusions have not been severed, one still does not transcend the conventional (*prajñapti*).
Why is this? Although one may benefit others while harming oneself, appearing to possess great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), it is still not truly great compassion.

It still does not bring great benefit. Although one must preach the Dharma while free from the body of mixed poisons, when Master Zhiyi of Ling Shan was approaching the end of his life, he humbly remarked regarding his own station that he had led the assembly too early.
He said that even those in the fifth grade who hold provisional positions might fear that their renunciation and preaching of the Dharma were not sincere.
When the Great Being of the Four Reliances, Bodhisattva Deva, was about to enter parinirvāṇa, [he spoke likewise].
He said to his disciples: "I previously intended to deliver others, yet my own station was not yet established. A Bodhisattva is humble and does not debate with ordinary people;
for these reasons, I did not preach the Dharma. Since my renunciation, I have not yet given rise to the mind of preaching the Dharma based on signs."
"What desire could possibly arise today? When the śramaṇa Śāntamati spoke these words, the class of bhikṣus who preached the Dharma with limited wisdom felt profound shame and remorse;
tears flowed from their eyes as blood, and they forever severed their intention to preach the Dharma or engage in formal debate."
I asked again, saying: "Although my mind has faith, I still give rise to doubt and confusion. Among all the merits of hearing the true teaching, preaching the Dharma for others is the foremost good.
As the Lotus Sūtra says: 'To secretly preach even a single phrase of the Dharma for the sake of a single person.'"
This person is an emissary of the Tathāgata who carries out the Tathāgata’s work; how much more so when they extensively expound it for others amidst the great assembly? Furthermore, a sutra states:
"If someone were to offer exquisite seven-jeweled treasures to all sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions for many eons, their merit would be exceedingly vast."

If there is a bhikṣu who explains even a four-line verse of the Dharma for the sake of a single sentient being, his merit surpasses the former [merit of building stūpas], being boundless, inexhaustible, and beyond comparison.
Furthermore, a sūtra states: "Among all forms of giving, the gift of the Dharma is supreme.
Since the assembly of bhikṣus constantly practices the gift of the Dharma, preaching the Dharma for others by such causes and conditions is the most supreme of deeds, as the Great Teacher has taught.
"This is a most grave matter. I am confused regarding the two paths and have not yet attained certainty; I pray that you will explain it to me.
The bhikṣu replied, "Since you are able to ask about this matter, I shall explain it for you. The Buddha said, "A bhikṣu maintains the precepts and is fully endowed with pure deportment."
Such bhikṣus all deserve to be honored; one should follow all that these bhikṣus practice. They are true sons of the Buddha;

they are true practitioners of the holy life (brahmacarya). Those who, being deluded by this principle, break the precepts and lack shame, whose mental conduct is undisciplined—they are not called śramaṇas.
They are not included in the number of the Saṃgha; they are not permitted to dwell together nor to practice together.

Although the great earth is vast and the waters of the ocean are many, for a monk who has broken the precepts, not even a single step of ground or a single drop of water is permitted. Such a person is a great and evil thief.

Since all that they employ is stolen, why is it permitted for them to preach the Dharma therein? Judging by this, one should know that the various sūtras spoken by bhikṣus were all composed by bhikṣus who maintain the precepts;
they were not permitted to be composed by bhikṣus who have broken the precepts, nor was it permitted for bhikṣus who have broken the precepts to preach the Dharma.
How much more so regarding the conduct of a Dharma-preacher who expounds the Lotus Sūtra!

Taking compassion as one’s dwelling, patience as one’s robe, and the emptiness of all phenomena as one’s seat—to dwell therein and preach the Dharma—is this not the conduct of a monk who has broken the precepts?
Therefore, you should not give rise to doubt. When preaching the Dharma, do not harbor expectations.
"Except for great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), he does not give rise to conceptual thoughts; as a bhikṣu whose inner and outer self is pure, he preaches the Dharma.
As for other śramaṇas, what kind of Dharma do they preach? I asked again: "I have now given rise to faith and no longer harbor doubt.
If you wish to preach the Dharma, with what kind of mind do you speak it for others? The bhikṣu replied: "There is no need for you to ask this. Why is that?"
To preach the Dharma and deliver sentient beings, seeking their fundamental causes and conditions is a great Buddha-activity, for it is the practice of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
For this reason, the Great Master Śākyamuni taught the methods for establishing [the practice] for those who rely upon the four reliances (*catur-yoniśaḥ-pratipatti*).
As detailed within the "Dharma Master" and "Peaceful Bliss" chapters of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he minutely explained the internal and external methods of practice. It is also like...
In various passages throughout other sūtras, the Buddha has taught the skillful means (*upāya*) for preaching the Dharma. Why then do you trouble me with this question? It may be answered as follows:
If one wishes to preach the Dharma, one should do so as the Buddha has taught; if one deviates from the Buddha’s teaching, one should not preach the Dharma at all. I further asked:

"As the Great Master has said, the skillful means for preaching the Dharma are clearly seen in the various sūtras. A śramaṇa who upholds the precepts is pure both internally and externally; however, [if he acts otherwise]..."
With great compassion and without harboring expectations, one preaches the profound and wondrous Dharma amidst the great assembly.

When there are those who pose difficult questions, one answers with a serene countenance and does not give rise to resentment; this is what it means to preach the Dharma. It is by such a method that one preaches the Dharma within the assembly.

For those of our kind—bhikṣus of inferior faculties who are attached to signs and violate the precepts—it is not possible to give rise to the conceptualization of "preaching the Dharma," much less preach it for the sake of a single person.
Beyond this, one should dwell in silent mountain forests, in places devoid of people.
"But I alone dwell in my own practice; having disciplined and composed my deluded mind, I do not preach the Dharma. How should I proceed?
I pray that you will explain this essential teaching for us. The śramaṇa replied, "Excellent, bhikṣu! You are a true son of the Buddha."
In this degenerate age of the final dharma, those who violate the precepts and preach the Dharma or engage in debate with only a fraction of wisdom do not know the proper direction.
Hearing such impure preaching, one’s karmic retribution becomes profound and heavy, leading to the arising of fear and the permanent cessation of preaching.

However, because of past habitual cultivation when first resolving for the Path, there may still be those who preach; yet, if such [preaching] still manifests before one, one should collect the mind, sit quietly upon the seat, and remain in silence.
This is the place where one should give rise to the contemplative mind and maintain the dignified demeanor of preaching the Dharma. Why is this? I have profoundly realized the Buddha's teaching;
having traversed the realm of the myriad dharmas and constantly contemplating the nature of the mind, I have reached the precious destination. I shall now explain this method for you.
The bhikṣu straightens his body, sits peacefully without moving, closes his eyes, and reflects, not directing his attention toward external objects. He should contemplate in this way:
"My own body is the Buddha-hall; who else outside the body could seek the path of the Buddha? The two legs are the pillars, and upon them rests the transverse backbone."
The two shoulder-beams of the ridgepole, with various other bones and tendons as the structural framework, skin and blood as the plastering and whitewashing;

because of the jewel upon its head, it places itself within the hall. The hollow interior of its belly is like the interior of the hall; the nine orifices on its body are like the doors and windows of the hall;
and the internal bones and flesh, which mutually partition one another, are like the inner and outer furnishings within a Buddhist shrine. Five.
The various organs and viscera, as well as all manner of substances—blue, yellow, red, white, long, short, square, and round; these diverse forms and colors fill its interior.
It is like the interior of a hall where banners, canopies, flower garlands, Buddha altars, and high seats are arranged and adorned with various precious objects.
Within this hall of the body is the *amala-vijñāna*, the Dharma-realm nature, the originally awakened *dharmakāya*. (30)
Surrounded by a retinue of seven, he sits in the full lotus posture upon a Dharma-lotus pedestal purified by samādhi.
The Dharma Master, the Sovereign King of the Sixth Consciousness, dons the robe of patience and wears the garment of compassion.

With the majestic deportment of the Dharma-gate purified, he pays homage to the Buddha of Original Enlightenment, confesses the transgressions of delusion, ascends the seat of Dharma-emptiness, and sits in tranquil composure as the Sovereign King of the Mind.
The Dharma Master saw within the hall that the fourfold assembly was seated together in a crowded manner.

These were the dharmas of the wholesome and unwholesome mental factors, namely the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*). Wholesome and unwholesome minds arise in constant association within the body, just as humans and devas of various types, with their mixed wholesome and unwholesome minds, are present at the Dharma seat to hear the teaching.
The great wholesome ground factors (*kuśala-mahābhūmika-dharma*), however, are associated only with wholesome minds.

They also arise within the body. Just as monastics, whether monks or nuns, have physical forms that accord with the Buddha and are present at the Dharma seat, so too do the great and small afflictions—greed, anger, and delusion—arise solely from an evil mind within the body.

Furthermore, just as beings such as ghosts, animals, and asuras, though they are sentient beings of the evil realms burdened by sinful karma, may still attend the hearing of the Dharma due to the presence of a karmic opportunity.

Seated. Regarding such categories of wholesome and unwholesome mental factors (*caitta*), within the assembly of the sixth consciousness, the Dharma Master—the Sovereign Mind—using the sound of the Great Dharma, without harboring fear or conceiving expectations, addressed the mental factors, saying:
"Listen well! I shall proclaim for you the Dharma-gate of the purity of the *tathatā* (suchness) of the Dharma-realm. Your own essential nature is itself the Buddha."

Dharma. Greed is the Way; so too are hatred and delusion. If this is so even for the collection of unwholesome mental factors (*citta-samprayukta-dharma*), how much more so for the collection of wholesome mental factors?

Are they not the Buddha? Each and every mental factor is fully endowed with the Buddha-dharmas, adorned with myriad virtues, indestructible and imperishable, without deficiency or diminution, wondrous and inconceivable—even including all the physical forms within the body-temple.
Dust, feet, pillars, flesh, walls, and all phenomena of form—each and every one is the *dharmadhātu-tathatā* (the suchness of the realm of phenomena). They do not obstruct one another;
they are perfectly interfused and sovereign. You, as mental factors (*caitta*), regarding the dharmas of the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), should no longer dwell in notions of individuality.

Due to the causal conditions of the power of deluded discrimination (*vikalpa-karma*), there arise the mind-king (*cittarāja*) and mental factors, along with their proximate and remote objects of perception (*ālambana*). At that moment...

At that very moment, the conditioned characteristics of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing, as well as impermanence and outflow (āsrava), when examined in their fundamental nature, are empty, quiescent, and of one suchness.
Who is the sovereign mind (cittarāja)? Who are the mental factors (caitta)? What is the original enlightenment, the Dharmakāya Tathāgata?
What is the physical body that serves as the monastery? Like a dream, like a shadow, and also like space—this is the inconceivable oneness.

Just as with the dharma-realm, when the Dharma Master, the Sovereign King of Mind, the sixth consciousness, expounded this teaching, the great assembly of mental factors (caitta) all attained the joy of the Dharma.
The hosts of greed, anger, and other afflictions were freed from their poisonous evils and were all transformed into practices such as generosity and compassion.
The virtuous mental factors—faith, diligence, wisdom, and so forth—increase immeasurable merit even further, and they pay reverent homage to the Sovereign King of Mind.
With reverence and respect, at that moment the body-hall suddenly became vast and expansive, its measure equal to the *dharmadhātu*.
The *āmalaka*-consciousness—the *dharmakāya* of original enlightenment and the Tathāgata of the four wisdoms—emitted the light of wisdom, illuminating the entire realm.

All Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and holy sages of the entire *dharmadhātu* came together and assembled, sitting within the body-hall. Thereupon, they immediately conferred their seal of approval upon the sixth consciousness, the mental faculty (*manas*).

The Dharma Master Śikṣācitta-rāja is like the occasion when Vairocana, within the womb of Māyā, preached the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, at which time all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas gathered together in a formal assembly.
The Dharma Master Śikṣācitta-rāja is illuminated by the light of the five wisdoms of original enlightenment and receives the seals of approval and praise from all Buddhas;
leaping with joy, he prostrates and pays homage to the Dharma of original enlightenment.
He circumambulated his own body and all the Buddhas a hundred thousand times, then withdrew to stand to one side. He again awakened to the profound Dharma-gate of the primordial limit (*mūlakoṭi*).
He perceived that the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is not separate from his own body, and that the clouds of gathered Buddhas are not separate from his own mind.

It is simply one sameness, like empty space; it does not cling to the extreme of existence, nor does it cling to the extreme of emptiness, nor does it give rise to the notion of both existence and non-existence.

It is neither non-existent nor existent; it is free from the attachments of the two extremes. It is utterly remote from the four propositions and the hundred negations, darkly accords with True Suchness (Tathatā), and abides therein in its full clarity.
To observe and contemplate the nature of the mind in this manner is called the true teaching of the Dharma.
You śramaṇas, practicing in this way, shall sever the afflictions. Thereafter, you may preach the Dharma-gate for the great assembly. O Bhikṣus, you should...
"Know this: this is the secret, most ultimate teaching on the contemplation of the mind. Do not let it be disclosed.
At that time, having heard this, I deeply received and upheld it. You, monks, should early on distance yourselves from fame and profit regarding the teaching of the Dharma;

you should deeply collect and compose your body and mind, fully maintaining the prohibitive precepts, so that you may achieve success in both worlds and undergo no suffering. Having heard this, the monks distanced themselves from [unwholesome states].
One should purify the discourse on the Dharma and its meaning, contemplate the Buddha-way without frequenting villages, and thereby attain the vision of the Buddha-body.

For this reason, one should know that the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings are non-differentiated in these three respects. One should contemplate the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the dharma-nature as quiescent, for all phenomena arise from the mind in an inconceivable manner.
